candidate.title: Unauthenticated open UDP reflector via forged AddrMangle destination in PunchHoleSent.socket_addr
candidate.component: hbbs rendezvous server - UDP message handler
candidate.root_cause: handle_hole_sent in rendezvous_server.rs does not verify that the AddrMangle-encoded destination in PunchHoleSent.socket_addr corresponds to any peer that actually participated in the rendezvous flow (AddrMangle::decode has no MAC/key binding - it is pure reversible arithmetic that anyone can compute), allowing any UDP client to make the server emit a PunchHoleResponse UDP packet to an arbitrary third-party IP:port of the attacker's choosing.
candidate.entry_point: Any internet host sending a RendezvousMessage::PunchHoleSent over UDP to hbbs's main rendezvous port (pre-auth, trust boundary 1) - the phs.socket_addr protobuf bytes field is fully attacker-controlled.
candidate.sink: socket.send(&msg_out, addr_a).await in handle_hole_sent (line 634), where addr_a = AddrMangle::decode(&phs.socket_addr) (line 615) is derived directly from attacker-supplied bytes with no validation.
candidate.trace: handle_udp (rendezvous_server.rs:431-433, RendezvousMessage::Union::PunchHoleSent arm) -> handle_hole_sent(phs, addr, Some(socket)) (rendezvous_server.rs:608) -> AddrMangle::decode(&phs.socket_addr) (line 615, lib.rs:161-184, no integrity check) -> socket.send(&msg_out, addr_a) (line 634) delivers a PunchHoleResponse (incl. relay_server, and a signed pk if phs.version/id resolve) directly to the attacker-chosen address.
candidate.attack: Attacker computes bytes b such that AddrMangle::decode(b) == victim_ip:victim_port (trivial: number = (victim_ip_u32 << 49) | (0 << 17) | victim_port, encode as 16 little-endian bytes, no need to reverse-trim). Attacker sends a small UDP PunchHoleSent{socket_addr: b, id: <any>, version: <any>} packet to hbbs's rendezvous port. hbbs replies with a PunchHoleResponse UDP packet sent straight to victim_ip:victim_port. Repeating this at line rate turns hbbs into an unauthenticated, no-spoofing-required UDP reflector that can flood an arbitrary third party with server-originated traffic; observed result is a PunchHoleResponse packet delivered to an address the attacker never legitimately interacted with.
candidate.preconditions: default config: yes - no licence_key check exists in this code path (only handle_punch_hole_request checks the -k key; handle_hole_sent does not). Requires only that the UDP rendezvous port is reachable, which is the default pre-auth deployment.
candidate.confidence_reason: Directly readable in source: AddrMangle::decode/encode is pure invertible arithmetic with no secret key (confirmed in libs/hbb_common/src/lib.rs:127-184), and handle_hole_sent has no auth/rate-limit gate before calling socket.send to the decoded address.

verdict.reason:
Every element of the claim is directly verifiable in the cited source with no unseen-layer assumption needed.

1. Reachability: `io_loop`'s UDP arm (rendezvous_server.rs:259-266) calls `self.handle_udp(&bytes, addr.into(), socket, key)` on every UDP datagram received on the rendezvous socket with zero pre-dispatch filtering (no `check_ip_blocker`, no rate limit, no key check before the match). Inside `handle_udp`, the `PunchHoleSent(phs)` arm (line 431-433) unconditionally calls `self.handle_hole_sent(phs, addr, Some(socket)).await?` — confirming this is pre-auth-reachable from any internet host, matching the stated trust boundary.

2. No auth gate on this path: the `key` parameter is threaded into `handle_udp` (line 322) but is never referenced anywhere in `handle_udp`'s body (verified by full read of lines 317-472) or in `handle_hole_sent` (608-639). The only place `ph.licence_key != key` is checked is `handle_punch_hole_request` (line 682), which is a *different* message type (`PunchHoleRequest`) whose UDP variant is explicitly disabled ("UDP PunchHoleRequest is intentionally unsupported", line 428-429). `PunchHoleSent` — TCP (527-529) and UDP (431-433) alike — never passes through that check. This directly confirms the claim's "no licence_key check exists in this code path" assertion.

3. Sink matches exactly: `handle_hole_sent` line 615 `let addr_a = AddrMangle::decode(&phs.socket_addr);` then line 634 `socket.send(&msg_out, addr_a).await?;` inside `if let Some(socket) = socket`. Both cited line numbers are correct verbatim.

4. AddrMangle has no integrity binding: read `libs/hbb_common/src/lib.rs:127-184`. `encode`/`decode` is pure reversible arithmetic on a u128 built from IP, port, and a truncated timestamp — no HMAC, no server secret, no nonce validation. I hand-verified the claim's simplified forging formula (set tm=0 ⇒ `number = (ip<<49)|port`) against the real `decode()` bit math and it correctly recovers the chosen ip:port with no need to reproduce `encode()`'s timestamp handling, confirming any external party can compute bytes that decode to an arbitrary victim IP:port.

5. Proto field confirms attacker control: `libs/hbb_common/protos/rendezvous.proto:50-56` defines `PunchHoleSent.socket_addr` as `bytes` with no companion signature/MAC field.

Net effect: an unauthenticated UDP client can send a minimal `PunchHoleSent{socket_addr: <forged bytes>}` datagram to hbbs's rendezvous port and cause the server to emit a `PunchHoleResponse` UDP packet directly to a third-party address of the attacker's choosing — a genuine confused-deputy / reflection primitive (CWE-406-style), not dependent on any code outside these files.

The only soft point is `potential_severity: Critical` — pure unauthenticated reflection/DoS-class primitives with no C/I impact on hbbs itself and no code-execution path typically cap around CVSS High (~7.5), not Critical, under standard scoring; I'd treat "Critical" as an optimistic upper bound rather than a hard error, so I'm not downgrading the verdict to "corrected" over it — the root cause, trace, and reachability are all exactly as claimed.
verdict.observed_mitigation: None found. The `key`/licence-key check exists only in `handle_punch_hole_request` (line 682) and does not run in the code path that handles `PunchHoleSent` (TCP at 527-529 or UDP at 431-433); `handle_hole_sent` itself has no auth, source-validation, or rate-limit gate before the `socket.send(&msg_out, addr_a)` at line 634.
verdict.live_test: On a running hbbs instance (no `-k` key needed since PunchHoleSent never checks it), from an attacker host: craft a minimal RendezvousMessage protobuf with union=PunchHoleSent{socket_addr: <16 bytes forged so AddrMangle::decode yields VICTIM_IP:VICTIM_PORT>} (e.g. bytes = little-endian 16-byte encoding of ((victim_ip_u32 as u128) << 49) | (victim_port as u128)), send it via UDP to hbbs:21116 (default rendezvous port) from a source address that is NOT victim_ip. Run a UDP listener (nc -ul <victim_port>) on VICTIM_IP and confirm it receives a PunchHoleResponse protobuf packet sourced from hbbs's IP:port shortly after the attacker's packet is sent, despite the attacker's socket never having contacted VICTIM_IP. Vulnerable: victim listener receives the reflected packet. Safe/patched: hbbs either rejects the message (auth error) or the packet is not delivered to VICTIM_IP.

verdict.reason:
Re-read rendezvous_server.rs in full. The claim's mechanics are accurate and provable from the cited artifacts: handle_udp (line 434-436) dispatches any UDP RendezvousMessage::LocalAddr with zero authentication straight to handle_local_addr(la, addr, Some(socket)) (line 642). Inside it, addr_a = AddrMangle::decode(&la.socket_addr) (line 649) is fully attacker-controlled — AddrMangle::decode (libs/hbb_common/src/lib.rs:161-184) is a pure bit-unshuffle with no HMAC/signature/session binding to any real prior exchange, so any byte string an attacker chooses decodes to an arbitrary IPv4 or IPv6 SocketAddr of their choosing. The server then unconditionally does socket.send(&msg_out, addr_a).await (line 666) — an exact match for the claim's cited sink line. No mitigating check exists between decode and send: the only rate-limiter in the file, check_ip_blocker, is wired only into the RegisterPk arm (line 350) and is never called for LocalAddr/PunchHoleSent. get_pk (line 1196) short-circuits to an empty Bytes when la.version is empty (which the attacker fully controls), so the packet costs the attacker nothing to send and requires no registered peer ID. This is genuinely pre-auth, default-config, and identical in root-cause shape to handle_hole_sent — confirmed, not refuted.

However the severity is overstated. PunchHoleResponse.socket_addr is set to la.local_addr.clone() and relay_server to la.relay_server — both fields the attacker supplies verbatim in the same UDP datagram that triggers the send. There is no server-side data that inflates the reply beyond what the attacker already paid for in the request (pk stays empty unless the attacker also supplies a real already-registered peer id AND the server was started with a signing key, in which case at most a small fixed ~100-byte signed IdPk blob is added). So the request:response byte ratio is roughly 1:1, not an amplifier (unlike NTP monlist/memcached-class bugs that justify Critical). The real, provable impact is a source-IP-spoofing/reflection primitive (attacker can make hbbs deliver a UDP packet to an arbitrary third party without revealing their own IP, and can fan this out across every public hbbs on the internet with zero registration and zero throttling) rather than a bandwidth-amplification DoS engine.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: Confirmed as stated: handle_local_addr (rendezvous_server.rs:642-671) blindly trusts la.socket_addr as a legitimate AddrMangle-encoded peer address and forwards a PunchHoleResponse to it with no correlation to any prior FetchLocalAddr the server itself issued, no signature/session binding in AddrMangle, and no rate limiting on this UDP arm — so it is a pure unauthenticated third-party-delivery (reflection) primitive. It is not, however, a bandwidth amplifier: the variable-length reply content (local_addr, relay_server) is attacker-supplied in the very packet that triggers it, so response size tracks request size roughly 1:1.
verdict.observed_mitigation: None present on this specific path (no check_ip_blocker / rate limiter is invoked for LocalAddr or PunchHoleSent in handle_udp, unlike RegisterPk at line 350) — the only correction here is to the severity/amplification framing, not the existence or reachability of the bug.

candidate.title: Unbounded global PUNCH_REQS Vec growth with trivially-bypassable dedupe and no rate limit on TCP PunchHoleRequest
candidate.component: hbbs rendezvous server - punch-hole request audit log
candidate.root_cause: handle_punch_hole_request in rendezvous_server.rs does not bound the size of the global PUNCH_REQS Vec (only manual admin 'pr -' clears it) and its dedupe check only scans the most recent 30 entries (lock.iter().rev().take(30)), so an attacker who rotates through 31+ target ids defeats the dedupe entirely, and there is no rate limit at all on TCP PunchHoleRequest (check_ip_blocker is only called from the UDP RegisterPk path), allowing unbounded memory growth and serialized global-Mutex contention.
candidate.entry_point: Any TCP client sending RendezvousMessage::PunchHoleRequest to hbbs's main TCP port (pre-auth, or bypassing the optional licence_key which is normally distributed to all legitimate clients as public config) targeting any currently-online peer id.
candidate.sink: lock.push(PunchReqEntry{...}) at rendezvous_server.rs:724, appending to the process-lifetime global static PUNCH_REQS: Lazy<TokioMutex<Vec<PunchReqEntry>>> (declared line 69) with no capacity cap.
candidate.trace: handle_tcp (rendezvous_server.rs:485-492, PunchHoleRequest arm) -> handle_tcp_punch_hole_request (line 849) -> handle_punch_hole_request (line 674) -> PUNCH_REQS.lock().await (line 716) -> dedupe scan over last 30 entries only (lines 718-723) -> lock.push(...) (line 724).
candidate.attack: Attacker self-registers 31+ peer ids (or reuses any 31+ known-online ids) and opens one raw TCP connection to hbbs, then blasts PunchHoleRequest messages in round-robin order across those ids as fast as the socket allows. Because each id's prior PUNCH_REQS entry is always pushed out of the 30-entry recent window before it repeats, dup never triggers and every single request appends a new PunchReqEntry (three owned Strings + an Instant) to the unbounded global Vec, which is also serialized behind one process-wide Mutex, so sustained flooding both grows heap usage without bound and stalls every other client's punch-hole processing that must also acquire PUNCH_REQS. Observed result: continuous growth of server memory and increasing latency/lock contention for all legitimate punch-hole requests until OOM or operator intervention via the 'pr -' admin command.
candidate.preconditions: default config: yes for the missing rate limit / unbounded growth; requires target ids to be currently 'online' (elapsed < REG_TIMEOUT), trivially satisfied by self-registering attacker-controlled peers via heartbeat.
candidate.confidence_reason: Directly readable: PUNCH_REQS is a plain Vec with no cap, dedupe window is hardcoded to 30, and no check_ip_blocker or any other throttle call exists anywhere on the TCP PunchHoleRequest code path.

verdict.reason: Verified line-by-line against the source: PUNCH_REQS is declared `static PUNCH_REQS: Lazy<TokioMutex<Vec<PunchReqEntry>>> = Lazy::new(|| TokioMutex::new(Vec::new()))` (line 69) with no capacity cap; the dedupe check at lines 716-724 in handle_punch_hole_request scans only `lock.iter().rev().take(30)` before unconditionally `lock.push(...)`ing at line 724 — confirmed exact match to the cited line. The only code that ever clears/trims PUNCH_REQS is the `punch-requests`/`pr` admin command (line 1042-1058, `lock.clear()` on `pr -`), and that admin listener (handle_listener2, lines 1094-1109) is restricted to `ip.is_loopback()` connections only — so no network attacker can trigger the reclaim. I confirmed check_ip_blocker (line 883) has exactly one call site in the whole file, at line 350, inside the UDP RegisterPk arm of handle_udp — it is never called anywhere on the TCP PunchHoleRequest path (handle_tcp -> handle_tcp_punch_hole_request line 849 -> handle_punch_hole_request line 674), so the "no rate limit on TCP PunchHoleRequest" claim is accurate. handle_listener_inner (line 1144) has no per-message throttle beyond a 30s idle read timeout, so a single TCP connection can fire PunchHoleRequest messages back-to-back at line rate. I also verified the precondition: PUNCH_REQS is only appended when pm.get(&id) succeeds AND elapsed<REG_TIMEOUT (line 697-709) — i.e. the target id must be a genuinely registered, recently-active peer — otherwise the function returns OFFLINE/ID_NOT_EXIST before reaching the record block, so the attacker does need >=31 peer ids they keep "online," which is achievable by self-registering/heartbeating their own fake peers as the claim states. All cited line numbers (69, 674, 716-724, 849, 883, 350) check out exactly. One mechanism detail in the claim is overstated: because the dedupe scan is capped at the most recent 30 entries (not proportional to total Vec length), per-request Mutex hold time stays roughly constant as PUNCH_REQS grows — it does NOT "increasingly stall" other clients' punch-hole processing as size grows; only the unbounded heap footprint (eventual OOM) is the real consequence of growth, not progressively worsening lock latency. This is CWE-400/CWE-770 unauthenticated remote resource exhaustion (availability-only impact — no path to confidentiality/integrity/code-execution), which caps CVSS around 7.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/A:H) — "High," not the claimed "Critical" potential.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: handle_punch_hole_request (rendezvous_server.rs:674) records every non-duplicate PunchHoleRequest into the process-lifetime global `PUNCH_REQS: Lazy<TokioMutex<Vec<PunchReqEntry>>>` (line 69, no capacity bound) via `lock.push(...)` at line 724, gated only by a dedupe check that scans just the most recent 30 entries (`lock.iter().rev().take(30)`, lines 718-723) — trivially defeated by rotating across >=31 distinct target ids. check_ip_blocker (the only throttle in the file, line 883) is called solely from the UDP RegisterPk arm of handle_udp (line 350) and is never invoked on the TCP PunchHoleRequest path, so an attacker who maintains >=31 self-registered "online" peer ids (elapsed<REG_TIMEOUT, confirmed required at line 702-709) can flood one raw TCP connection with round-robin PunchHoleRequest messages, unboundedly growing PUNCH_REQS with no automatic eviction — the only reclaim is the `pr -` admin command (line 1046), reachable only via the loopback-restricted debug listener (handle_listener2, line 1097 `ip.is_loopback()`), i.e. unreachable to a remote attacker. Because the dedupe scan window is fixed at 30 regardless of total Vec size, per-request lock hold time does not scale with growth — the deliverable impact is unbounded heap growth toward OOM, not progressively increasing lock-contention latency as the original claim implies.
verdict.corrected_severity: High (base) — potential/worst-case capped at High, not Critical, since impact is availability-only (unauthenticated remote memory exhaustion / process crash) with no confidentiality, integrity, or code-execution path.
verdict.live_test: On a test hbbs instance with no -k license key configured: (1) self-register 32 fake peer ids via RegisterPk/RegisterPeer UDP messages, re-heartbeating each every <30s to keep them "online"; (2) open one raw TCP connection to hbbs's main port and send PunchHoleRequest{id: peer_i} in round-robin order across all 32 ids as fast as possible for e.g. 60s; (3) via the loopback-only admin console (`pr 0 999999`) or a debug build, observe PUNCH_REQS.len() growing roughly 1:1 with requests sent and never shrinking. Vulnerable: PUNCH_REQS length grows unbounded and process RSS increases monotonically with sustained flooding, with no self-imposed cap. Safe/patched: PUNCH_REQS length plateaus at a fixed cap (e.g., LRU-evicted or bounded ring buffer) regardless of sustained flooding, or requests are throttled/rejected after a per-IP rate threshold before reaching the push.

candidate.title: BytesCodec used with no max_packet_length cap on the pre-auth TCP rendezvous listener - single 4-byte header triggers up to ~1GB allocation
candidate.component: hbbs rendezvous server - TCP frame decoder
candidate.root_cause: handle_listener_inner constructs Framed::new(stream, BytesCodec::new()) without ever calling set_max_packet_length, so BytesCodec::max_packet_length stays at its default usize::MAX (bytes_codec.rs:29); decode_head() then calls src.reserve(n) for any attacker-supplied length prefix n up to 0x3FFFFFFF (~1GiB, bytes_codec.rs:60-64) before any of the actual payload bytes have been received, letting a 4-byte header force a ~1GiB buffer reservation per TCP connection.
candidate.entry_point: Any TCP client connecting to hbbs's main rendezvous TCP port (pre-auth) and sending a 1-4 byte length-prefix header claiming a large frame size.
candidate.sink: src.reserve(n) inside BytesCodec::decode_head (libs/hbb_common/src/bytes_codec.rs:64), invoked transitively by the Framed stream constructed at rendezvous_server.rs:1180 with no length cap configured.
candidate.trace: handle_listener (rendezvous_server.rs:1134) -> handle_listener_inner (line 1144) -> Framed::new(stream, BytesCodec::new()).split() (line 1180, no set_max_packet_length call anywhere in the codebase - confirmed via grep) -> b.next() drives BytesCodec::decode -> decode_head (bytes_codec.rs:41) -> src.reserve(n) with n up to 0x3FFFFFFF (bytes_codec.rs:60-65).
candidate.attack: Attacker opens a TCP connection to hbbs's rendezvous port and sends a single crafted 4-byte length prefix (e.g. head_len selector bits set to 3, encoding n=0x3FFFFFFF after the >>2 shift) without sending any further payload bytes. The codec immediately reserves ~1GiB of heap for that connection before any data has arrived. Opening a modest number of such connections (tens to low hundreds, well within default OS/file-descriptor limits) exhausts server memory and crashes or OOM-kills hbbs, a pre-auth remote denial of service triggered by only a handful of bytes per connection.
candidate.preconditions: default config: yes - set_max_packet_length is never called anywhere in the entire rendezvous_server.rs or hbb_common tree (verified by grep), so every TCP-framed listener (main port and the ws-upgraded WebSocket path uses a different codec, but the raw TCP path at line 1180 is fully exposed) inherits the unbounded default.
candidate.confidence_reason: Grep-confirmed absence of any set_max_packet_length call in the codebase combined with reading decode_head's reserve(n) logic and the encoder's own 0x3FFFFFFF max representable length; the only uncertainty is real-world allocator/OS behavior under the reservation (may fail gracefully on some platforms rather than OOM, but resource exhaustion via many connections remains valid regardless).

verdict.reason: Fully re-derived from source, no unseen layer required. (1) rendezvous_server.rs:1180 constructs Framed::new(stream, BytesCodec::new()) with no set_max_packet_length call — grep across the entire codebase (including libs/hbb_common) shows set_max_packet_length is defined (bytes_codec.rs:37) but never called anywhere, so BytesCodec keeps its default max_packet_length = usize::MAX (bytes_codec.rs:29). (2) This Framed stream is reached from io_loop's listener.accept() (line 300-311) on the main rendezvous TCP port with zero auth/size-negotiation gate — genuinely pre-auth. (3) bytes_codec.rs decode_head (lines 41-66) parses a 1-4 byte length header, checks n > max_packet_length (always false with usize::MAX default), then unconditionally calls src.reserve(n) — this executes purely from the header, before decode_data requires any further payload bytes. Max representable n with a 4-byte header is 0x3FFFFFFF (~1 GiB), matching the encoder's own ceiling (bytes_codec.rs:127-128). (4) No rate-limiting/connection-cap code guards this path — the only IP-blocker in the file (check_ip_blocker, ~line 883) gates the UDP registration path, not TCP accept. The claim's title, trace, sink, and root_cause all check out verbatim against the code. Only soft nuance: BytesMut::reserve is a capacity grow (likely mmap-backed, not necessarily instant RSS-resident), so "instantly consumes ~1GiB physical memory per connection" slightly overstates the mechanism of impact — real-world effect is more likely either gradual RSS growth as pages get touched, or (in memory-constrained containers) an immediate allocation-failure abort, which is if anything a faster single-connection DoS than described. This doesn't change that it's a genuine, unauthenticated, uncapped-allocation resource-exhaustion bug (CWE-770) reachable with a single 4-byte packet.
verdict.corrected_severity: High (matches candidate's own severity field; potential_severity=Critical is unsupported — this is a pure resource-exhaustion/DoS primitive with no demonstrated path to memory corruption or RCE, so Critical as a "potential" ceiling should be walked back to High/Medium-High depending on operational deployment memory limits)
verdict.corrected_root_cause: Root cause as stated is accurate: BytesCodec::new() defaults max_packet_length to usize::MAX and rendezvous_server.rs:1180 never calls set_max_packet_length before wrapping the pre-auth TCP listener stream, so decode_head's src.reserve(n) is bounded only by the wire format's own ~1GiB ceiling, not by any application-level cap. Minor refinement: characterize the impact as "unbounded per-connection allocation request with no application-imposed cap" rather than asserting a guaranteed ~1GiB physical RSS consumption per connection, since bytes::BytesMut::reserve is a capacity reservation whose physical-memory materialization is allocator/OS-dependent (may fail fast via abort in memory-constrained deployments, or grow RSS gradually as touched) — both outcomes are still valid DoS vectors, just via slightly different failure modes than "OOM-kill after tens to hundreds of connections."
verdict.observed_mitigation: None found. Verified absence of set_max_packet_length calls via full-tree grep, and absence of any rate-limit/connection-cap/IP-blocker gate on the TCP accept path (listener.accept() -> handle_listener -> handle_listener_inner) prior to the Framed/BytesCodec construction at line 1180.
verdict.live_test: On a running hbbs instance bound to port P (default 21116): open a raw TCP connection to P and send exactly the 4 bytes 0xFF 0xFF 0xFF 0x3F (little-endian u32 = 0x3FFFFFFF, low 2 bits = 0b11 selecting 4-byte head_len, decoded n = 0x3FFFFFFF >> 2... actually to select head_len=4 and maximize n, send bytes [0xFF,0xFF,0xFF,0xFF] which gives head_len=(0xFF&0x3)+1=4, n=0xFFFFFFFF>>2=0x3FFFFFFF) then send no further bytes and hold the connection open. Vulnerable result: process RSS/VSZ for the hbbs PID (via `ps -o rss,vsz -p <pid>` or /proc/<pid>/status VmRSS/VmSize) jumps immediately after the 4 bytes are read, before any additional payload is sent (observable via strace -e trace=mmap,brk,recvfrom on the hbbs process, or cgroup memory.current under Docker). Safe/patched result (after adding codec.set_max_packet_length(some_bound) before Framed::new): the same 4 bytes cause the connection to be dropped with an "Too big packet" InvalidData error (bytes_codec.rs:61) instead of any large reserve.

candidate.title: WebSocket listener trusts client-supplied X-Real-IP/X-Forwarded-For headers with no trusted-proxy check, enabling IP spoofing of all downstream address-based logic

The cited code is exactly as claimed: make_pair_ (line 425-462) reads the first frame from any pre-auth TCP/WS connection, parses it as a RendezvousMessage, and if it is a RequestRelay union member (protobuf field `licence_key` is `string`, confirmed in libs/hbb_common/protos/rendezvous.proto:109), does `if !key.is_empty() && rf.licence_key != key { ...; return; }` at line 430. This is Rust's default String/str PartialEq (byte-slice comparison), which is not constant-time (length-dependent early exit, and in practice content-dependent exit behavior via memcmp/vectorized-compare codegen) — this is a correct, verifiable code-level fact, not an assumption about an unseen layer. Entry-point reachability is also verifiable: handle_connection (line 359-391) only filters IPs already present in an operator-maintained BLOCKLIST (line 382) before spawning make_pair for every other client; there is no rate limiting, no per-connection minimum-delay padding, and no length-independent/constant-time comparison anywhere in this file or in the flow leading to line 430. So I cannot refute on 'entry not reachable' or 'mitigation present' grounds — both are contradicted by the code I read. The claim's own precondition (`-k <key>` must be set; skipped when key is empty) is also correctly derived from `!key.is_empty()` at line 430 and matches get_server_sk's handling (line 568-587). What remains genuinely unverifiable from source alone is the *practical* exploitability of the timing side channel itself — whether an attacker over a real network (even LAN) can extract a statistically significant per-byte timing signal above jitter/scheduling noise to actually recover the licence_key. That is an empirical, runtime property (network stack behavior, actual key length/entropy, TLS/WS framing overhead, OS scheduler noise) that cannot be settled by reading relay_server.rs — it requires actual timing measurements against a running hbbr instance. The claim's own confidence (0.3) and disposition_hint ('needs-live-validation') already reflect this correctly; I concur rather than override it. Root cause, entry point, sink, and trace as stated are all accurate; only the 'enables ... key recovery' framing in the title is an unproven empirical claim, which the candidate itself hedges appropriately.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: No correction needed to the root cause as stated — confirmed accurate: relay_server.rs:430 `rf.licence_key != key` is a non-constant-time String inequality performed on an attacker-supplied field of the first pre-auth frame, with no rate limiting or timing-normalization anywhere upstream in handle_connection/make_pair/make_pair_.

verdict.observed_mitigation: None found. handle_connection (relay_server.rs:359-391) only rejects IPs already present in the manually curated BLOCKLIST set (line 382); it applies no rate limiting, connection throttling, or constant-time delay before dispatching to make_pair_. The comparison at line 430 uses the language-default String inequality with no length pre-normalization or constant-time primitive (e.g. no subtle::ConstantTimeEq, no `ring::constant_time::verify_slices_are_equal` equivalent) anywhere in this file.
verdict.live_test: Build hbbr from targets/rustdesk-server with a known licence key, e.g. `cargo run --bin hbbr -- -k TESTKEY0123456789ABCDEF` (default relay TCP port 21117, confirmed via utils.rs:115 doctor_tcp reference and hbbr.rs RELAY_PORT). Write a minimal client using hbb_common's length-prefixed bytes_codec framing (matching libs/hbb_common/src/tcp.rs FramedStream) that connects over raw TCP to 127.0.0.1:21117 and sends a RendezvousMessage{ union: RequestRelay{ licence_key: <guess>, uuid: "" } } for two guess groups, N=5000 trials each, interleaved to cancel drift: Group A = keys sharing the first 20 of 24 correct bytes (`rf.licence_key` matches key[0..20]) with the last 4 bytes wrong; Group B = keys with 0 correct leading bytes (completely wrong, same total length as the real key). Measure wall-clock delta from `connect()` completion to socket EOF/RST (the server returns without writing any response on mismatch, so timing is via connection-close latency, not payload). Run first on loopback (best case for the attacker) then again from a separate host on the same LAN segment. Compute Welch's t-test / Mann-Whitney U between Group A and Group B latency distributions. Vulnerable result: p < 0.01 with Group A (more correct prefix bytes) showing a consistent, reproducible delta of even single-digit microseconds to low-milliseconds versus Group B, stable across repeated runs — this would support incremental prefix recovery. Safe/non-exploitable result: no statistically significant separation between groups beyond scheduler/network noise floor even on loopback, i.e., the per-byte signal is smaller than achievable measurement resolution — which is the expected outcome for short in-process comparisons over any real socket path, and would downgrade this from a practical attack to a code-quality/defense-in-depth finding only.

candidate.title: PeerMap::get_or grows the in-memory peer cache unbounded for any non-existent id — memory-exhaustion DoS
candidate.root_cause: get_or (peer.rs:157-169) inserts a brand-new default Peer entry into self.map (an unbounded HashMap<String, LockPeer>) for every id that is not already cached or present in the database, with no cap, TTL, or eviction policy anywhere in this file, so a stream of lookups against distinct, never-registered ids permanently grows server memory.
candidate.entry_point: the target id field of any pre-auth rendezvous message that triggers a peer lookup for a non-existent id (e.g. punch-hole/connect-to-peer requests naming an arbitrary target id)
candidate.sink: peer.rs:167 `w.insert(id.to_owned(), tmp.clone());` — permanent, uncapped insertion into self.map
candidate.trace: attacker sends repeated requests referencing distinct random ids -> rendezvous_server.rs (out of scope) calls PeerMap::get_or(id) [peer.rs:158] -> self.get(id) misses both cache and DB [peer.rs:159 / 136-155] -> falls through to double-checked insert of a new default LockPeer [peer.rs:162-168] -> entry retained forever, no eviction anywhere in this file
candidate.attack: Attacker sends a high-rate stream of connection/punch-hole requests each naming a distinct, never-registered numeric id (trivially enumerable, e.g. sequential or random 9-digit strings). Each miss permanently adds an entry (String key + Arc<RwLock<Peer>>) to the server's in-memory map. Sustained traffic drives unbounded RSS growth until the hbbs process is OOM-killed, denying service to all legitimate peers.
candidate.preconditions: requires the caller in rendezvous_server.rs to invoke get_or (rather than a read-only get) on attacker-influenced target ids without a pre-check that the id is a real, previously-seen peer. default config: yes, no cap exists in this file
candidate.confidence_reason: the unbounded-growth mechanism itself is 100% visible in get_or; whether/how attacker-controlled arbitrary ids reach get_or in volume depends on rendezvous_server.rs call sites not in this slice

verdict.reason: The core mechanism claimed for get_or (peer.rs:157-169) is verified accurate: on a total miss (not in map, not in DB) it unconditionally inserts a default Peer into self.map with no cap/TTL, and a full-repo grep confirms nothing anywhere ever calls .remove() on that map — entries live forever. That much is CONFIRMED. However the claim's entry-point/attack narrative is factually wrong and must be corrected. get_or has exactly one call site (rendezvous_server.rs:353), inside the RegisterPk UDP handler, where `id` is the peer's own self-chosen registration id (rk.id) — NOT a punch-hole/connect-to-peer 'target' id as the claim states. I verified the actual punch-hole path (handle_punch_hole_request, rendezvous_server.rs:697) calls self.pm.get(&id) — the read-only lookup (peer.rs:136-155) — which does NOT insert on a total miss (falls through to `None` at line 154 with the map untouched). So the claim's specific stated attack ('high-rate stream of connection/punch-hole requests each naming a distinct, never-registered id') does not trigger this bug at all. Additionally, the claim's precondition field ('no cap exists in this file... default config: yes') is misleading: the real call site IS gated, per source IP, by check_ip_blocker (rendezvous_server.rs:883-911) — max ~30 RegisterPk requests/60s AND a hard cap of 300 new distinct ids per 24h per source IP, after which further novel ids from that IP are rejected before ever reaching get_or. So a single-source flood is capped at ~300 new heap entries/day, not unbounded. The bug is still real and pre-auth reachable (uuid/pk just need to be non-empty, id just needs len>=6, no auth token required) and the per-IP throttle is bypassable at scale via a botnet or UDP source-IP spoofing (insertion happens synchronously on packet receipt, before any reply, so no return-path is needed for the attack to succeed) — both standard low-bar techniques against an internet-facing pre-auth UDP daemon. So this downgrades from 'uncapped/unthrottled DoS via punch-hole target ids' to 'throttled-but-bypassable unbounded growth via the self-registration id field of RegisterPk', which is a real, correctable finding at a different call site than claimed.

verdict.reason: The core code-level observation is accurate: create_tables (database.rs:74-84) declares `id varchar(100)` / `note varchar(300)`, but SQLite VARCHAR(N) is type-affinity only and never enforced as a length constraint, and insert_peer (database.rs:106-125) binds id/uuid/pk/info via sqlx::query! with zero application-level length check before the INSERT. That part is confirmed. However the claim overstates worst-case impact and understates an observable mitigation it explicitly flagged as unverified: (1) RegisterPk is handled exclusively via the UDP path (rendezvous_server.rs handle_udp, dispatch at line 342 -> update_pk at 418 -> PeerMap::update_pk in peer.rs:93-133 -> Database::insert_peer). hbb_common's FramedSocket for UDP (libs/hbb_common/src/udp.rs) delivers one datagram per message with no length-prefix framing, so each RegisterPk's id+uuid+pk payload is hard-capped by the UDP datagram limit (~65507 bytes), not the 'kilobytes/megabytes' the claim implies. (2) check_ip_blocker (rendezvous_server.rs:883-911), invoked at line 350 before any insert, throttles by source IP to at most 30 register_pk requests per 60s and at most 300 NEW distinct peer ids per 24h; only requests that pass this gate reach update_pk/insert_peer. This is exactly the layer the claim's own preconditions/confidence_reason said was 'out of scope' — I read it and it is a real, present mitigation, not an unobserved layer, so this is not needs-live-validation. verdict.reason:
Re-read common.rs in full plus main.rs and hbb_common::version_check_request. Every code-level claim checks out exactly as stated, with no observed mitigation:

1. common.rs:195-198 — outer `std::thread::spawn(move || loop { ... })` calls `std::thread::spawn(move || allow_err!(check_software_update_()))` (line 196) every 24h and discards the inner JoinHandle — no `.join()` anywhere in the function. Confirmed unbounded, un-reaped thread spawn.
2. common.rs:201-210 — `check_software_update_` is `#[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]`, so each invocation runs its own dedicated OS thread + runtime. `reqwest::Client::builder().build()?` (line 204) has no `.timeout()`/`.connect_timeout()` call, nor is `.timeout()` chained on the request builder. reqwest's documented default is no timeout at all, so `.send().await?` / `.bytes().await?` (lines 207-210) can block the thread indefinitely if the peer completes the TCP/TLS handshake but withholds the HTTP response.
3. main.rs:34 — `crate::common::check_software_update();` is called unconditionally at hbbs startup with no CLI flag or config gate in the observed arg list — confirms "default config: yes."
4. hbb_common/src/lib.rs:426 — the destination is a hardcoded HTTPS URL (`https://api.rustdesk.com/version/latest`), not attacker-influenced. Since reqwest validates TLS certs by default (no `danger_accept_invalid_certs` set), this is a materially narrower precondition than a generic on-path attacker implies: triggering requires either compromising RustDesk's own official update-check server, or an attacker holding a CA-trusted certificate for that specific domain (DNS hijack alone is insufficient) — the claim's own text already states this precondition, which I can't refute as wrong, only confirm as narrow.

I could not find any timeout, join, cap, or opt-out anywhere in this file or main.rs that would refute the claim. candidate.title: Unsanitized external update-check URL fragment written to server log (log forging)

verdict.reason:
Re-read common.rs:193-218 line by line. The claim's mechanics are accurate: resp.url (from serde_json::from_slice of the raw HTTP response body, common.rs:211) flows unsanitized through response_url.rsplit('/').next() (line 213) straight into log::info!(\"new version is available: {}\", latest_release_version) at line 215 — no CR/LF filtering, no character allow-list, anywhere in the chain. flexi_logger (used by hbbs/main.rs, hbbr.rs) does no control-character escaping when writing to the log sink, so this is a genuine log-injection primitive if the response body is attacker-controlled.

I verified the one part the claim only asserted by example rather than proving: whether the version-number gate at line 214 (get_version_number(latest_release_version) > get_version_number(VERSION)) can actually be satisfied while still carrying a CRLF payload. Read hbb_common::get_version_number (lib.rs:249-274): it splits on '-' first, uses only the first two '-'-delimited tokens for the numeric comparison, and the doc comment literally says \"// Ignore the rest\". So a payload like \".../1.99.0-0-\\r\\n[forged log line]\" parses \"1.99.0-0\" as a high version number (passing the gate) while the full string including the CRLF-injected tail is still what gets passed whole to log::info! (latest_release_version is the entire post-slash substring, not truncated to the parsed portion). So the gate is bypassable — the claim's PoC sketch would work mechanically.

What the claim under-specifies, and what I can refute as an *observed mitigating fact* (not an assumed one): the request in check_software_update_ is not to an attacker-suppliable or configurable URL — hbb_common::version_check_request (lib.rs:426) hardcodes URL = \"https://api.rustdesk.com/version/latest\", and the reqwest::Client is built with reqwest::Client::builder().build()? — no .danger_accept_invalid_certs(), no custom root store, no cert-bypass anywhere in the crate (grepped for danger_accept_invalid/accept_invalid/tls bypass across all .rs files; the only TLS code found, in proxy.rs, uses rustls_platform_verifier / native_tls::TlsConnector::new() — standard validation, unrelated to this call path). So this is a normal TLS-verified HTTPS request to a hardcoded, well-known domain. The claim's framing (\"an on-path/MITM attacker... returns a JSON body\") undersells the actual precondition: a bare on-path/network MITM position is NOT sufficient against a cert-validated HTTPS connection — the attacker needs either a CA-trust-level compromise (mis-issued/trusted-root cert) or actual compromise of RustDesk's own api.rustdesk.com backend, i.e. a supply-chain-level precondition, not casual network MITM.

Net effect: the vulnerable code mechanism is 100% confirmed statically (bad sink, verified bypass of the version gate), but the entry-point/precondition description needs correcting to reflect the much harder bar (CA compromise or official-backend compromise, not on-path MITM), which the claim's own Low severity / 0.25 confidence / needs-live-validation hint already implicitly account for, so this does not change the severity rating — it stays Low, matching the claim's self-assessment, and the impact ceiling is genuinely capped at forged lines in hbbs's own local log file (no format-string risk in Rust's format!, no evidence in this codebase of automated downstream parsing/alerting on this specific log line, so the \"SOC/SIEM triage confusion\" framing is speculative amplification beyond what the code shows).
verdict.corrected_root_cause: check_software_update_ (common.rs:201-218) sends a TLS-certificate-validated HTTPS POST to the hardcoded https://api.rustdesk.com/version/latest (hbb_common::version_check_request, lib.rs:425-426, via a default reqwest::Client with no cert-validation bypass anywhere in the crate). The JSON response's `url` field is deserialized (line 211) and, without any sanitization, response_url.rsplit('/').next() (line 213) is logged verbatim via log::info! (line 215). The version-number gate at line 214 is bypassable: hbb_common::get_version_number (lib.rs:249-274) only consumes the first two '-'-delimited tokens of the string and explicitly \"ignore[s] the rest\", so a crafted segment like \"1.99.0-0-\\r\\n<forged log line>\" both defeats the gate (parses as a high version) and still logs its full CRLF-laden tail verbatim (flexi_logger performs no control-character escaping). The real precondition is therefore not mere network MITM but TLS-trust-level compromise (a mis-issued/trusted-root certificate) or actual compromise of RustDesk's own api.rustdesk.com backend — a supply-chain-class precondition, not casual on-path interception.
verdict.live_test:
Cannot be safely live-tested against the real api.rustdesk.com (would require either forging a trusted TLS cert for that domain or compromising RustDesk's actual infrastructure — out of scope/illegal to attempt). Safe local equivalent: patch a local build's version_check_request() URL constant to point at a test HTTPS server you control with a self-signed cert trusted only in a throwaway trust store, have that server return {"url":"https://x/1.99.0-0-
[FORGED] fake admin login accepted
"} from /version/latest, run check_software_update_() with RUST_LOG=info, and inspect the resulting log file/stdout. Vulnerable: the raw CR/LF and forged text appear as literal embedded newlines/content inside the log stream (a forged-looking extra log line). Safe/patched: the sink would strip or escape control characters (e.g. .replace(['','
'], "") or a %? escape) before logging, so the CRLF/forged text shows as a single sanitized line with no injected line breaks.
verdict.observed_mitigation: reqwest::Client::builder().build()? in check_software_update_ (common.rs:204) uses default TLS certificate validation with no .danger_accept_invalid_certs() or custom trust anchor anywhere in the crate (verified by grep across all .rs files); the destination URL is hardcoded to https://api.rustdesk.com/version/latest (hbb_common::lib.rs:426), not attacker-suppliable. This raises the real precondition from "on-path/MITM" (as the claim states) to "TLS-trust-level compromise or official-backend compromise" — the claim's severity/confidence were already conservative enough (Low/0.25) that this correction narrows the framing without changing the numeric rating.

candidate.title: get_expired_time silently collapses expiry threshold to 'now' on Instant underflow
candidate.root_cause: get_expired_time in common.rs does not distinguish a genuine underflow failure from a valid 1-hour-ago Instant -- Instant::now().checked_sub(Duration::from_secs(3600)).unwrap_or(now) silently substitutes 'now' (i.e. a zero-second window) whenever the process/monotonic clock has been running for under 3600s, rather than signaling the caller that no reliable expiry threshold could be computed, allowing any time-window/replay/re-registration gate elsewhere in the server that is built on this primitive to unexpectedly narrow to zero width during that startup period.
candidate.entry_point: Server process uptime < 3600s (e.g. immediately following any restart, including one an attacker could help induce via an unrelated crash/DoS bug) combined with any caller-side comparison of a peer/session timestamp against this function's return value; the exact consumer of get_expired_time() lives in rendezvous_server.rs, which is outside this slice, so the attacker-facing sink cannot be independently cited here.
candidate.sink: Whatever comparison in the (out-of-slice) rendezvous/registration logic uses get_expired_time()'s return value as an expiry/replay threshold -- not directly visible in common.rs/utils.rs/main.rs/lib.rs.
candidate.trace: get_expired_time() (common.rs:15-19) computes threshold -> returned to an unseen caller in rendezvous_server.rs -> caller compares some peer-supplied/recorded timestamp against the threshold to decide expiry/dedup/replay handling.
candidate.attack: During the first hour after any hbbs restart, if any registration-throttling or replay-window logic depends on get_expired_time() returning a genuine 1-hour-ago timestamp, it instead receives 'now', which could either mass-expire all just-registered peers or (depending on comparison direction, unverified) weaken a re-registration/anti-flood gate, letting an attacker flood registrations more aggressively than intended in that window.
candidate.preconditions: Server uptime < 3600s; exact security consequence depends entirely on unseen consumer code in rendezvous_server.rs; default config: yes (function has no feature gate).
candidate.confidence_reason: Root-cause code (the underflow fallback) is directly citable and is a real logic flaw, but the actual dangerous sink/consumer is outside this file slice so the concrete security consequence is unverified -- flagged per the hunt lens rather than fully proven.

verdict.reason: The cited code is accurately quoted (common.rs:15-19, get_expired_time() = Instant::now().checked_sub(Duration::from_secs(3600)).unwrap_or(now)) and is a real logic flaw. Tracing the caller (which the candidate flagged as unverified) resolves the two open questions: (1) the consumer is Peer::default() in peer.rs:48/55 (last_reg_time, reg_pk), used pre-auth in rendezvous_server.rs's handle_punch_hole_request (elapsed()>=REG_TIMEOUT check, line 700-702) and handle_online_request (line 793-797, reachable via the unauthenticated OnlineRequest handler at line 1124-1126 in handle_listener2 with no auth check). (2) the actual effect is the OPPOSITE of both hypotheses in the claim: because reg_pk.0 starts at 0 regardless of the fallback timestamp, the register_pk rate-limiter is unaffected on the first call (no flood-enabling or mass-expiry). What actually happens is that a freshly-loaded (never-registered-this-run) Peer gets last_reg_time=now instead of now-3600s, so elapsed()<REG_TIMEOUT (30s) for up to 30 seconds after object creation -- the peer is falsely reported ONLINE / non-expired rather than expired. Additionally, the claim's entry-point framing is factually wrong and independently disprovable: get_expired_time() relies on Rust's Instant, which on Linux/macOS/Windows is a system-wide monotonic clock tied to host boot (CLOCK_MONOTONIC / mach_absolute_time / QueryPerformanceCounter), not a per-process clock -- restarting/crashing the hbbs process does NOT reset it, so an attacker cannot induce the underflow window via a DoS/crash-restart of hbbs as claimed; it can only occur in the first hour after the underlying host/kernel actually boots, a far narrower and much less attacker-controllable precondition.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: get_expired_time() (common.rs:15-19) silently substitutes Instant::now() for the intended "1 hour ago" whenever now.checked_sub(3600s) would underflow. Since Instant is a boot-relative (not process-relative) monotonic clock on all major platforms, this window only exists in the first hour after the host machine itself boots -- NOT after a plain hbbs process restart/crash, contrary to the claim's entry-point framing. When it fires, the confirmed effect (traced through peer.rs:48/55 -> rendezvous_server.rs:700-702/793-797, both reachable pre-auth) is that a Peer object created during that window has last_reg_time=now instead of now-3600s, so it is erroneously reported as ONLINE/not-expired (elapsed()<REG_TIMEOUT=30s) for up to 30 seconds per peer-object-creation event, via the unauthenticated OnlineRequest and PunchHoleRequest handlers -- the opposite of the claim's speculated "mass-expire" effect. The reg_pk register_pk rate-limit gate is unaffected in practice since reg_pk.0 starts at 0 regardless of the fallback timestamp.
verdict.observed_mitigation: None present in code -- this is a genuine (if narrow) logic bug, not fully mitigated. However the claim's own worst-case hypotheses (registration flood, mass-expiry) do not occur: reg_pk.0 is initialized to 0 regardless of the timestamp so the anti-flood gate is unaffected on first use.
verdict.live_test: Not required to reach a verdict -- the caller code is fully visible in-repo (peer.rs, rendezvous_server.rs) and the platform behavior of std::time::Instant (boot-relative monotonic clock, unaffected by process restart) is documented Rust stdlib semantics, so this was resolved analytically rather than needing runtime validation.

candidate.title: max_packet_length cap is dead code: no caller ever restricts frame size below the wire-format ceiling (~1.07GB), enabling pre-auth per-connection memory exhaustion against hbbs/hbbr and clients
candidate.component: hbb_common::bytes_codec::BytesCodec (shared by rustdesk-server hbbs/hbbr and the RustDesk client)
candidate.root_cause: decode_head in bytes_codec.rs does not enforce any meaningful upper bound on the attacker-declared frame length `n` before entering DecodeState::Data(n), because `self.max_packet_length` defaults to `usize::MAX` (see `BytesCodec::new()`, line 32) and `set_max_packet_length()` (line 40-42) is never invoked anywhere in either the RustDesk client repo or the rustdesk-server repo -- confirmed via `rg -n set_max_packet_length` across both trees, which returns only the method's own definition. The `if n > self.max_packet_length` gate at line 63 is therefore unreachable dead code in every real deployment, allowing any peer to declare and have accepted a frame length up to the wire format's own ceiling of 0x3FFFFFFF (~1.07 GB, the max representable value for a 4-byte head_len=4 header per the `n >>= 2` encoding).
candidate.entry_point: The first 1-4 bytes of any TCP/websocket stream framed with `BytesCodec` -- i.e. any pre-auth inbound connection to hbbs (rustdesk-server/src/rendezvous_server.rs:1180, `Framed::new(stream, BytesCodec::new())`) or hbbr (rustdesk-server/src/relay_server.rs, via `hbb_common::tcp::FramedStream`), or a malicious/MITM rendezvous server or remote peer's response stream to a RustDesk client (libs/hbb_common/src/tcp.rs `FramedStream::new`/`from`/`connect`, all using bare `BytesCodec::new()`). This is the attacker-controlled length header byte(s) parsed by decode_head.
candidate.sink: BytesMut accumulation in `decode()`/`decode_data()` (bytes_codec.rs lines 76-81, 105-114): once `DecodeState::Data(n)` is set, the codec keeps returning `Ok(None)` and letting the underlying `Framed`/tokio buffer grow until `src.len() >= n`, i.e. it buffers up to the attacker-declared `n` (max ~1.07GB) bytes per connection before ever validating that this is a legitimate/expected size for the protocol state the connection is in.
candidate.trace: 1) BytesCodec::new() (bytes_codec.rs:28-34) leaves max_packet_length=usize::MAX. 2) rendezvous_server.rs:1180 wraps every accepted pre-auth TCP connection with `Framed::new(stream, BytesCodec::new())`, no set_max_packet_length call. 3) rendezvous_server.rs:1180-1183 drives the codec via `timeout(30_000, b.next()).await` in a loop. 4) tokio_util FramedRead -> BytesCodec::decode() (bytes_codec.rs:88-115) -> decode_head() (44-74) parses the attacker's header, computes n up to 0x3FFFFFFF, the dead check at line 63 never rejects it, sets DecodeState::Data(n). 5) subsequent decode() calls -> decode_data() (76-81) keep returning None while `src` (the connection's read buffer) grows toward n bytes as the attacker (optionally very slowly) trickles data, consuming heap memory for the life of the connection (bounded to 30s by rendezvous_server's own timeout, but re-triggerable by reconnecting or by holding many connections in parallel).
candidate.attack: Attacker = any anonymous internet host, no registered ID or auth token needed. It opens a raw TCP connection to hbbs's client-facing port (default 21116) or hbbr's relay port (default 21117) and sends a 4-byte header such as bytes [0xFF,0xFF,0xFF,0xFF]: head_len=(0xFF&0x3)+1=4, raw 32-bit value 0xFFFFFFFF, n = 0xFFFFFFFF >> 2 = 0x3FFFFFFF (~1.07 GB). decode_head() accepts this unconditionally (the size gate never fires because max_packet_length is never lowered from usize::MAX). The connection's buffer then grows toward ~1GB as the attacker sends data (or repeats this across many parallel/short-lived connections), applying sustained memory pressure to the pre-auth hbbs/hbbr process that all RustDesk clients rely on for NAT traversal and relay -- an unauthenticated remote DoS vector against core infrastructure. Observed from source: decode_head's own designed safety valve (max_packet_length) is provably never wired up by any of the ~9 BytesCodec instantiation sites found via grep.
candidate.preconditions: Default config: yes. No authentication required (pre-auth TCP listener on hbbs/hbbr). Requires the attacker to sustain many concurrent connections or repeated reconnects to accumulate meaningful aggregate memory pressure, since (a) the speculative pre-allocation in decode_head is already correctly capped to MAX_PREALLOCATED_PAYLOAD_LEN=256KB (mitigating a single-packet huge-alloc/RUSTSEC-2026-0007-style crash), and (b) rendezvous_server.rs applies a 30s per-`.next()` timeout that eventually drops a stalled connection.
candidate.confidence_reason: The code-level defect (max_packet_length never configured away from usize::MAX) is directly provable via grep across both repos plus the read source; pre-auth reachability at hbbs/hbbr is directly cited. The magnitude of real-world memory-exhaustion impact (whether other layers such as OS connection limits or an unseen accept-rate limiter blunt it) requires live/dynamic confirmation, hence not higher.

verdict.reason:
Re-derived from raw source, not just the claim. All load-bearing facts check out:

(1) `BytesCodec::new()` (bytes_codec.rs:28-34) sets `max_packet_length: usize::MAX`. Confirmed by direct read.
(2) `set_max_packet_length()` (line 40-42) is a real, callable API — but `rg -n set_max_packet_length` across both `targets/rustdesk` and `targets/rustdesk-server` returns ONLY the method's own definition (in each repo's copy of hbb_common). No call site exists anywhere in either tree. So the `if n > self.max_packet_length` gate at line 63 is provably dead: `self.max_packet_length` is `usize::MAX` in every live instantiation, and the attacker-controlled `n` computed from a 4-byte head is bounded to 0x3FFFFFFF (~1.07GB) by the wire format itself (`n >>= 2` after reading up to 4 LE bytes) — always ≤ usize::MAX, so the check never fires.
(3) Pre-auth reachability confirmed for both daemons: hbbs `rendezvous_server.rs:1180` — `Framed::new(stream, BytesCodec::new())` on every accepted TCP connection before any auth; hbbr `relay_server.rs:420` — `FramedStream::from(stream, addr)` → `tcp.rs:136` `Framed::new(DynTcpStream(...), BytesCodec::new())`, also pre-auth (the RequestRelay/key check happens only after the first frame is fully decoded, i.e. after this codec already buffered it).
(4) `decode_data()` (76-81) does exactly what's claimed: returns `Ok(None)` and lets `src` keep growing until `src.len() >= n`, i.e. up to the attacker-declared `n` bytes are buffered before the frame is ever validated by any higher-layer check.
(5) The claim's own noted mitigations are real and correctly cited: `MAX_PREALLOCATED_PAYLOAD_LEN = 256*1024` (line 6, applied at 69-72) caps the *initial* speculative `reserve()` call, and a 30s timeout wraps frame reception on both hbbs (`timeout(30_000, b.next())`, rendezvous_server.rs:1182) and — I additionally verified — hbbr (`timeout(30_000, stream.recv())`, relay_server.rs's `make_pair_`). I found no additional hidden bound (no global connection-memory cap, no rate limiter gating this codec) in either file that the claim missed.

One refinement worth noting: the 30s timeout wraps the *entire* single `.next()`/`recv()` call that must produce one complete decoded frame, not a per-byte idle-timer — so to actually grow a connection's buffer close to the ~1.07GB ceiling the attacker must sustain high throughput (tens of MB/s) within that single 30s window, not merely dribble bytes indefinitely. This makes the primitive a bandwidth-symmetric (non-amplified) buffering DoS rather than a cheap Slowloris-style near-zero-cost hold — consistent with, and actually reinforcing, the claim's own conservative "Medium" (not "High") severity rating for realized impact, while "High" remains fair for the worst-case/aggregate-connections framing. No code-observable barrier refutes reachability or the missing bound; the only remaining unknown is real-world magnitude (OS/process memory limits, actual per-connection buffer growth rate under tokio), which is a severity-calibration question, not an existence question, and the claim already flagged that honestly.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: No correction to the stated root cause needed; refinement only — add that the 30s per-`.next()`/`recv()` timeout on both hbbs and hbbr bounds total single-frame receive time (forcing the attacker to sustain meaningful throughput to fill a large buffer in one connection) rather than merely gating long idle periods, and that hbbr (relay_server.rs `make_pair_`) has the identical 30s timeout pattern as hbbs, not just hbbs as the claim states.
verdict.observed_mitigation: Two real, code-confirmed partial mitigations already correctly credited by the claim: (a) MAX_PREALLOCATED_PAYLOAD_LEN=256KB caps the initial speculative BytesMut::reserve() in decode_head (bytes_codec.rs:69-72), preventing a single-shot huge-allocation crash; (b) a 30-second timeout wraps each full-frame receive on both hbbs (rendezvous_server.rs:1182, timeout(30_000, b.next())) and hbbr (relay_server.rs make_pair_, timeout(30_000, stream.recv())), which bounds how much data a single connection can accumulate per attempt to roughly (attacker sustained throughput × 30s), capped at ~1.07GB. Neither mitigation fully closes the gap: set_max_packet_length() is still never called anywhere, so no deployment-appropriate ceiling below ~1.07GB is ever enforced.
verdict.live_test: Against a disposable hbbs instance (or hbbr): open a raw TCP connection to the client port (default 21116 for hbbs / 21117 for hbbr), send the 4-byte header bytes 0xFF 0xFF 0xFF 0xFF (head_len=4, n = 0xFFFFFFFF >> 2 = 0x3FFFFFFF ≈ 1.07GB), then stream ~200MB of arbitrary filler bytes over ~15s while sampling the server process's RSS (e.g. `ps -o rss= -p <pid>` or /proc/<pid>/status VmRSS) every second. Vulnerable/expected-per-claim result: connection stays open (no "Too big packet" io::Error, no immediate reset) and RSS grows roughly in step with bytes sent, confirming decode_head accepted the ~1.07GB-class length header and decode_data is buffering toward it. Safe/patched result: connection is closed immediately after the 4-byte header with an "Too big packet" error and RSS stays flat, indicating set_max_packet_length() has been wired up to a sane per-deployment ceiling.

All are attacker-controlled bytes off the wire from the paired remote peer (trust boundary 3: remote peer -> controller / controller -> host), post-NaCl-handshake but with no size validation performed before decompression.

verdict.reason:
Re-read libs/hbb_common/src/compress.rs in full (34 lines). Line 32-34 is exactly as claimed:
    pub fn decompress(data: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8> {
        zstd::decode_all(data).unwrap_or_default()
    }
zstd::decode_all streams the input through a zstd Decoder until EOF, transparently walking concatenated frames, with no output-size ceiling, no ZSTD_d_windowLogMax tightening, and errors silently swallowed by unwrap_or_default(). This is a textbook unbounded-decompression sink (CWE-409). No wrapper, cap, or alternate "safe" decompress function exists anywhere in the tree — grepped all 9 call sites of hbb_common::compress::decompress and every one calls it directly on network-derived bytes.

Verified attacker reachability and the claimed absence of a size gate:
1. flutter.rs:666 `set_cursor_data(cd: CursorData)` calls `hbb_common::compress::decompress(&cd.colors)` UNCONDITIONALLY — no `compress`/size-flag check at all (unlike the clipboard paths). Same at ui/remote.rs:122 (Sciter UI). CursorData is a message the connected peer can send to the client with zero permission gating (no disable_clipboard/view_only style check exists for it).
2. The primary (non-Android/non-iOS) desktop clipboard path also decompresses unconditionally: src/clipboard.rs `from_clipboard()` (lines 715-720) — `if clipboard.compress { decompress(&clipboard.content) }` — feeding into `from_multi_clipboards`/`update_clipboard`, used on Windows/macOS/Linux, not just the ios/android branches originally cited in the claim's trace.
3. Server-side (host receiving from the controller in src/server/connection.rs) Clipboard/MultiClipboards handling IS gated behind `self.authorized` (confirmed at connection.rs:2835, wrapping the match arms at 3037/3065) plus `clipboard_enabled()`, matching the claim's own stated precondition — so that specific direction is correctly scoped as post-auth only.
4. Client-side (io_loop.rs `handle_msg_from_peer`, called unconditionally for every frame from `peer.next()` at line 256) has NO auth/login gate around the match: CursorData (line 1454) and Clipboard (line 1462) branches are reached regardless of `self.is_connected`, which is only set true deep inside the `LoginResponse::PeerInfo` arm (line 1450) — i.e. it is bookkeeping state, not a dispatch gate. This means a malicious/rogue peer that the client dials (or a MITM on an insecure connection) can send a CursorData message and trigger the unbounded decompress() BEFORE the client ever validates a password / receives a successful LoginResponse — a genuinely pre-auth-from-the-client's-perspective reachable path. The claim itself only speculated this ("unconfirmed without live state-machine tracing"); I was able to confirm it structurally from source (the dispatch match has no auth precondition), no runtime needed.

No mitigating layer was found: BytesCodec (bytes_codec.rs) caps only pre-allocation (MAX_PREALLOCATED_PAYLOAD_LEN=256KB) and enforces max_packet_length, but max_packet_length is set to usize::MAX by default and set_max_packet_length() is never called anywhere in the tree (grepped) — so the outer frame is bounded only by the ~1GB representable in the 4-byte varint header, and even that only caps the compressed input, not the decompressed output, which is unbounded regardless of ratio (zstd back-references within-window or multi-frame concatenation can expand a small compressed input to arbitrarily large output).

Net effect: the claim's core defect (unbounded zstd decode with no size ceiling) is proven purely from static source, not merely plausible-but-unverified. I additionally confirmed (rather than left as speculative) that the CursorData vector on the client is fully ungated and reachable pre-authentication, which the original claim had hedged as unconfirmed "potential Critical." I still assess it as High rather than Critical because the impact is pure availability (memory-exhaustion/OOM/hang of the client or host process) with no confidentiality/integrity compromise — consistent with standard CVSS treatment of unauth network DoS (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H ≈ 7.5), which the claim's own baseline "High" already reflects correctly; I would not inflate to Critical absent an actual C/I impact.

verdict.reason:
Re-read tcp.rs in full. The core code claim is accurate: Encrypt::dec (tcp.rs:301-315) does `if bytes.len() <= 1 { return Ok(()); }` before ever calling secretbox::open, and self.2 (the receive nonce counter) is NOT incremented in that branch, so a 0- or 1-byte frame is returned from FramedStream::next() unauthenticated. This is confirmed, reachable, and not gated by any check I can't observe.

However the severity/framing is wrong. Two things undercut the "auth-bypass" characterization:

1. Design intent for the <=1 branch is clearly the 0-byte heartbeat: secretbox::seal always appends a 16-byte MAC, so no legitimately-encrypted frame can ever be <2 bytes (in fact never <16). The heartbeat is sent as literal Bytes::new() via send_bytes() (bypassing Encrypt::enc entirely) at rendezvous_mediator.rs:455 and client.rs:4052, and every caller I found explicitly special-cases it with `bytes.is_empty()` (rendezvous_mediator.rs:452, client.rs:4051) BEFORE calling parse_from_bytes. So the 0-byte path is intentional protocol behavior, not a bypass.

2. The residual bug is genuinely that `<=1` is over-broad vs. the intended `==0`, letting a bare 1 unauthenticated byte slip through unchecked. But I traced every consumer of FramedStream::next()/conn.next() across src/client.rs, src/rendezvous_mediator.rs, src/common.rs, and src/server/connection.rs: none of them act on a 1-byte payload's content. Protobuf's wire format cannot encode any semantically meaningful/actionable field in 1 byte, so in every case the injected byte either (a) falls through the `is_empty()` heartbeat branch as a no-op (0-byte case), (b) fails Message/RendezvousMessage::parse_from_bytes and is silently dropped via `if let Ok(msg_in) = ...` in server/connection.rs:938 (completely benign), or (c) fails parsing and propagates via `?` in client.rs:4055 / rendezvous_mediator.rs:458 / common.rs:1235, tearing down just that one connection/future. That third outcome is the claim's own "demonstrated impact" (forced HC-connection teardown) — but an attacker in the stated MITM/malicious-rendezvous position already trivially owns that capability by just closing or RST'ing the TCP connection directly; the bug grants no new capability, no message forgery, no data exfiltration, and no path to controlling program behavior with attacker-chosen content. There is no scenario found where the smuggled byte is trusted as authenticated application data that drives a security decision.

So this is a real, code-verified robustness/invariant-violation defect (FramedStream::next() should only ever return authenticated bytes once secured, and the check should be `bytes.is_empty()` not `bytes.len() <= 1`), but it is not a Medium auth-bypass — it doesn't let an attacker inject or forge any meaningful authenticated-looking data, and the only observable effect (forced disconnect in 2 of 4 call sites) duplicates a capability the MITM/malicious-server attacker already has natively.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: Encrypt::dec's short-circuit `if bytes.len() <= 1 { return Ok(()); }` (tcp.rs:302-304) is meant to pass through the intentional, unencrypted 0-byte heartbeat frames (sent raw via send_bytes(Bytes::new()), bypassing Encrypt::enc, at client.rs:4052 and rendezvous_mediator.rs:455 — legitimate secretbox ciphertext is always ≥16 bytes so it can never collide with this range) but is written over-broadly as `<=1` instead of `==0`/`is_empty()`, so a literal attacker-injected 1-byte frame also skips secretbox::open with no MAC check. This is a genuine violation of the "next() only returns authenticated bytes once secured" invariant, but not an exploitable auth bypass: protobuf's wire format cannot encode any actionable field in 1 byte, and every consumer (client.rs hc_connection_, rendezvous_mediator.rs, common.rs post_request TCP-proxy path, server/connection.rs main loop) either drops the resulting parse failure silently or tears down only that one connection/future — an effect a MITM/malicious-server attacker can already achieve directly via TCP disruption, so no new capability is gained.

candidate.confidence_reason: The missing socket.connect() and the explicit '_' discard of the source address are directly cited from source; downstream unauthenticated dispatch to sensitive sinks (Config persistence, connect_tcp_local) is also directly cited. verdict.live_test: On a host running the rustdesk client with no rendezvous connection actually reachable (or intercept before the real server can respond), from a second attacker-controlled host send a forged RendezvousMessage protobuf (e.g. ConfigureUpdate{rendezvous_servers:['attacker.example.com'], serial: <current+1>}) via raw UDP to the client's ephemeral local UDP source port (observable via `ss -un` / `netstat -anu` on the client host, or by first sniffing the client's outbound REGISTER_PEER packet to learn its source port) addressed at the client's public/NAT-mapped IP:port. Vulnerable result: client log shows 'restart' triggered and `Config::get_rendezvous_servers()` now returns the attacker value (verify via the client's config file / `rustdesk --get-conf rendezvous-servers` or equivalent), despite the datagram never having come from the real rendezvous server IP. candidate.sink: socket_client.rs connect_tcp_local -> FramedStream::new(target, local, ms_timeout) (line 176) - outbound TCP connection to attacker-chosen destination

verdict.reason: All the cited code facts check out: connect_tcp_local (lines 150-178, verified) does no destination validation before FramedStream::new(target, local, ms_timeout) at line 176; handle_punch_hole in rendezvous_mediator.rs decodes ph.socket_addr via AddrMangle::decode (also unvalidated - verified lib.rs:176-199, any 4/16-byte payload decodes to an arbitrary IPv4/IPv6 SocketAddr with no range check) at line 651, and passes the result straight into socket_client::connect_tcp_local(peer_addr, Some(local_addr), 30) at line 713 with zero destination filtering.
