Net effect of this specific path: causes the client to emit a single blind outbound TCP SYN to an attacker-chosen host:port with no observable result - real but far lower impact than 'Medium/High SSRF... probe internal services'.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: connect_tcp_local/connect_tcp genuinely perform no destination-range validation (confirmed: no loopback/RFC1918/link-local check anywhere in socket_client.rs), and handle_punch_hole feeds it a rendezvous-server-controlled, unvalidated AddrMangle-decoded address (rendezvous_mediator.rs:651,713) - that part of the claim is accurate. But at this specific sink the resulting Stream is discarded unused and immediately dropped (never bound to a variable at line 713), and FramedStream::new performs only connect()+set_nodelay with no data exchange, and allow_err! suppresses any result from reaching the network. This is the code's documented hole-punching technique (comment at line 711), inherent to any NAT-traversal/ICE-style protocol that must dial peer-supplied addresses. So the finding is real as a 'missing internal-IP allowlist on outbound punch/dial helpers' hardening gap, but it does not grant response inspection, data exfiltration, or a usable port-scan oracle, and should not be framed as classic SSRF with High potential severity.

candidate.title: WsFramedStream::next() skips NaCl secretbox decryption/authentication for WebSocket Text frames
candidate.component: hbb_common::websocket (WS client transport used by rustdesk client to hbbs/hbbr)
candidate.root_cause: WsFramedStream::next in websocket.rs does not apply self.encrypt.dec() (NaCl secretbox authenticate-then-decrypt) to WsMessage::Text frames the way it does for WsMessage::Binary frames (compare lines 291-299 vs 300-303), allowing raw, unauthenticated attacker-supplied bytes to be returned to the caller and parsed as a legitimate decrypted peer message whenever the remote endpoint sends the payload as a Text opcode instead of Binary.
candidate.entry_point: Bytes received over an established WebSocket connection to the rendezvous/relay endpoint (hbbs/hbbr or a WS-fronting proxy in front of them) or from a relayed remote peer — trust boundaries #1/#2/#3 in the target description.
candidate.sink: The unauthenticated BytesMut is returned to the caller (Stream::next in stream.rs) and fed directly into protobuf::Message::parse_from_bytes(&bytes) at every conn.next() call site after conn.set_key() has been called (e.g. src/client.rs secure_connection at line 797 and all subsequent message-loop reads), which treats the bytes as an authenticated message from the trusted peer.
candidate.trace: remote WS endpoint sends opcode=0x1 (Text) frame containing crafted protobuf bytes -> tokio_tungstenite WebSocketStream::next() -> WsFramedStream::next() websocket.rs:290-303 matches WsMessage::Text arm, builds BytesMut from text.as_bytes() WITHOUT calling self.encrypt.as_mut().dec() -> returned as Ok(bytes) -> caller (e.g. src/client.rs:794-797, or the main message loop) calls Message::parse_from_bytes(&bytes) and processes it as a genuine peer message.
candidate.attack: WHO: the relay/rendezvous WS endpoint itself (meant to be an untrusted, blind relay of encrypted peer traffic per the target's own trust model: 'hbbr blindly relays encrypted streams'), or any active MITM able to inject frames on a ws:// (plaintext) session. EXACT INPUT: after a secure key has been negotiated (conn.set_key() called), send a WebSocket frame with opcode 0x1 (Text) whose payload is a serialized RustDesk protobuf Message (e.g. forged MouseEvent/KeyEvent/FileAction/ClipboardOperation) instead of the expected opcode 0x2 (Binary) that would normally be passed through secretbox decryption. OBSERVED RESULT: the client accepts and parses the forged message as if it had come through the authenticated, secretbox-protected channel — no decryption error, no rejection — because key.dec() is never invoked for this frame type.
candidate.preconditions: default config: no (the WS transport itself requires allow-websocket=Y, which is opt-in / not default, to be used at all). Once WS transport is active and a secure key has been established via set_key(), the bypass applies unconditionally with no further config needed.
candidate.potential_severity: Critical — full unauthenticated remote-control command injection to a controlled host, or forged screen/clipboard/file data to a controller, since this defeats the exact security property (relay cannot forge/tamper with encrypted peer traffic) the secretbox layer exists to provide over a WS-relayed session.
candidate.confidence_reason: The asymmetric handling (dec() called for Binary, not for Text) is directly visible and unambiguous in the file; residual uncertainty is only about how commonly WS transport + relay is deployed in practice and whether any additional validation exists further downstream in message handlers not reviewed in this slice.

verdict.reason:
Re-read /Users/krasn/tools/raptor/targets/rustdesk/libs/hbb_common/src/websocket.rs in full. The claim is accurate on every material point:

1. Asymmetric handling exists exactly as described (websocket.rs:290-303): the `WsMessage::Binary(data)` arm builds `bytes` and, if `self.encrypt.as_mut()` is `Some`, calls `key.dec(&mut bytes)` (returns `Err` on failure, line 293-297) before returning. The `WsMessage::Text(text)` arm (line 300-303) does `BytesMut::from(text.as_bytes())` and returns `Ok(bytes)` immediately — `self.encrypt` is never consulted at all for Text frames. This is not a logic error I need to infer; it is a direct textual omission of the encrypt check.

2. `Encrypt::dec` (tcp.rs:301-315) wraps `secretbox::open`, which is NaCl authenticated decryption (fails closed on a bad/missing MAC). So the Text-frame path genuinely skips both decryption and authentication, not just decryption — an attacker sending a Text frame supplies bytes that go straight from wire to "trusted, decrypted" status.

3. Contrast confirmed: `tcp::FramedStream::next()` (tcp.rs:178-188) applies `key.dec()` unconditionally to every message with no frame-type branch — the bypass is unique to the WS transport's opcode dispatch, not a generic pattern in the codebase.

4. Sink confirmed exactly as cited: `src/client.rs:794-797` (`secure_connection`) does `let bytes = res?; if let Ok(msg_in) = Message::parse_from_bytes(&bytes) { ... message::Union::SignedId ... }` and later sets `conn.set_key(key)` at line 810. The main post-handshake read loop at `src/client.rs:4048-4054` also calls `conn.next()` and processes `bytes` directly. Both are real call sites, not invented.

5. Reachability: `Stream::WebSocket(WsFramedStream)` (stream.rs:9-12) is the concrete backing when `connect_websocket` is used (stream.rs:92-102), and `Stream::next`/`set_key` forward transparently to the WS impl (stream.rs:58-65, 117-124). `check_ws`/`use_ws()` gate WS transport behind `allow-websocket=Y` (config.rs:2843-2846, option2bool treats `allow-*` keys as default-off unless `== "Y"`), so this is correctly flagged in the claim's own preconditions as non-default/opt-in — the claim does not misrepresent this as default-on.

6. Trust model fit: the task's own stated trust boundary #2 ("rendezvous server -> client (client trusts server messages)") is precisely the boundary this bug breaks — a malicious or MITM'd hbbs/hbbr WS endpoint (or an on-path attacker for plain `ws://`) can choose opcode 0x1 instead of 0x2 to inject unauthenticated bytes that the client treats as an authenticated peer message.

One nuance the claim doesn't spell out (a real but non-refuting constraint): WS Text frames must be valid UTF-8 per RFC 6455 / tungstenite, so an attacker's forged protobuf payload is constrained to byte sequences that are also valid UTF-8. That narrows, but does not eliminate, the exploitable message space (numeric/varint-heavy or short/ASCII-safe protobuf messages are easily crafted as valid UTF-8), and the claim's confidence (0.8, not higher) and "requires opt-in config" precondition already reflect appropriate hedging. This doesn't change the verdict.

No mitigating check exists anywhere in the read file or the two downstream call sites — this is a genuine, provable-from-artifacts auth-bypass in the opt-in WS transport of the RustDesk client.

candidate.title: TLS certificate validation fail-open with permanently cached insecure decision on first-contact MITM
candidate.root_cause: WsFramedStream::try_connect automatically retries a failed wss:// TLS handshake with danger_accept_invalid_certs=true whenever the per-URL TLS cache is empty (tls.rs::get_cached_tls_accept_invalid_cert returns None, which only happens when 'allow-insecure-tls-fallback' is enabled and the host is uncached), then unconditionally persists that relaxed decision via upsert_tls_cache() on the very connection attempt that used it — regardless of whether the original failure was caused by a legitimate certificate problem or an active on-path MITM presenting a bogus certificate — poisoning the client's TLS trust for that host indefinitely with no re-verification or expiry.
candidate.entry_point: An active network attacker positioned between the client and the rendezvous/relay wss:// endpoint during the client's first (uncached) connection attempt to that host, while the operator has 'allow-insecure-tls-fallback' enabled.
candidate.sink: Self::get_connector(TlsType::Rustls/NativeTls, danger_accept_invalid_certs=true) at websocket.rs:104/47-64, used to build the TlsConnector actually performing the (now non-validating) TLS handshake, followed by upsert_tls_cache(url, tls_type, true) at websocket.rs:112 which persists the bypass.
candidate.trace: wss:// handshake against MITM-presented cert fails (websocket.rs:105-110) -> match arm (TlsType::Rustls, _, None) at websocket.rs:116-131 -> recursive try_connect(..., danger_accept_invalid_cert=Some(true), ...) -> Self::get_connector(Rustls, true) builds a non-validating connector -> handshake against the MITM succeeds -> upsert_tls_cache(url, tls_type, true) at websocket.rs:112 makes the bypass permanent for that host.
candidate.attack: WHO: active network/MITM attacker (e.g. rogue AP, malicious router, TLS-intercepting proxy). EXACT: present an invalid/self-signed certificate during the client's very first wss:// connection attempt to a given rendezvous/relay host, with 'allow-insecure-tls-fallback' already enabled by the operator. OBSERVED: the client automatically disables certificate validation for that attempt, completes the TLS handshake with the attacker, and remembers (via the process-lifetime URL_TLS_DANGER_ACCEPT_INVALID_CERTS cache in tls.rs) to skip certificate validation for that host on all subsequent connections, even after the attacker is no longer on-path.
candidate.preconditions: config: allow-insecure-tls-fallback=Y is required (NOT default — default is off per option2bool's 'allow-' prefix rule requiring explicit "Y"); additionally requires no prior cached TLS decision for that host (first-contact / fresh cache, or after reset_tls_cache()).
candidate.potential_severity: Critical — complete, silently-persisted MITM of all subsequent traffic to that host once the insecure decision is cached, since nothing in this code path re-verifies or expires it.
candidate.confidence_reason: The retry/cache-poisoning mechanism is directly visible in websocket.rs; the gating condition (allow-insecure-tls-fallback, default off) was confirmed by cross-checking config.rs and tls.rs, which lowers likelihood but doesn't change the underlying logic flaw; did not confirm whether any UI warning accompanies the fallback.

verdict.reason: Full code trace confirms the claim's core mechanism is real, not hypothetical. websocket.rs:74-86 (connect()) calls get_cached_tls_accept_invalid_cert(url), which lives in tls.rs:83-98: when allow_insecure_tls_fallback() is false (config.rs:2848-2851, gated by option2bool's 'allow-' prefix rule => default OFF unless explicitly 'Y'), it unconditionally returns Some(false) -- never None -- regardless of cache state. That forces try_connect's match at websocket.rs:115-131 into the Some(_) arms, never the (Rustls,_,None) retry-with-invalid-certs arm at line 116. So with the feature off (default), the automatic downgrade path is provably unreachable -- this matches and confirms the claim's own confidence_reason. When allow-insecure-tls-fallback=Y IS set and the host is uncached, get_cached_tls_accept_invalid_cert correctly returns None, the (TlsType::Rustls,_,None) arm at line 116 fires on ANY handshake failure (cert error, MITM, or otherwise -- no differentiation, confirming fail-open-on-any-error as claimed), retries via get_connector(Rustls,true) -> verifier::client_config(true) -> client_config_danger() -> NoVerifier (verifier.rs:14-33), whose verify_server_cert unconditionally returns Ok(ServerCertVerified::assertion()) -- genuinely zero cert validation, not a partial check. On success, line 112 unconditionally calls upsert_tls_cache(url, tls_type, true), and tls.rs:42-61 persists that per-domain 'accept invalid certs' flag in a process-lifetime static RwLock<HashMap> with no expiry/re-verification, exactly as claimed. Correction to scope: the claim's preconditions section lists only allow-insecure-tls-fallback=Y, but WsFramedStream::try_connect is only reached at all when the endpoint has already been converted to a ws://wss:// URL, which check_ws()/use_ws() (websocket.rs:340-343, config.rs:2843-2846) gate behind OPTION_ALLOW_WEBSOCKET ('allow-websocket'), itself default-off via the identical 'allow-' prefix rule in option2bool. So exploitation actually requires TWO independent non-default flags (allow-websocket=Y AND allow-insecure-tls-fallback=Y) enabled simultaneously by the operator, not one. This doesn't invalidate the underlying logic flaw (which is real and exactly as described) but narrows the realistic attack surface further than the claim states, so severity is left unchanged but the missing precondition is flagged as a correction.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: Same mechanism as claimed (websocket.rs try_connect fail-open retry with danger_accept_invalid_certs=true on first TLS handshake failure, permanently cached via upsert_tls_cache at tls.rs, verified to be a genuine full cert-validation bypass via verifier.rs's NoVerifier), but reachability additionally requires OPTION_ALLOW_WEBSOCKET ('allow-websocket', default OFF) to be enabled so that WsFramedStream/wss:// is used at all, in addition to the already-cited OPTION_ALLOW_INSECURE_TLS_FALLBACK ('allow-insecure-tls-fallback', default OFF). verdict.reason:
Line 98 (`let ws_config = None;`) is real and confirmed — RustDesk never tunes a local WebSocketConfig for the WS transport. But two load-bearing parts of the claim's framing are wrong, verified by reading the actual pinned dependency source (tokio-tungstenite/tungstenite 0.26.2, matching Cargo.lock) and by grepping the whole target repo:

1) "relying solely on upstream tungstenite defaults" is true, but those defaults are NOT an absence of protection. Fetched tungstenite v0.26.2 src/protocol/mod.rs: `WebSocketConfig::default()` sets `max_message_size: Some(64<<20)` (64 MiB) and `max_frame_size: Some(16<<20)` (16 MiB). `WebSocketContext::new`/`from_partially_read` do `config.unwrap_or_default()`, so passing `None` resolves to these real limits, not `usize::MAX`. In `protocol/frame/mod.rs::read_frame` (fetched v0.26.2), the check `if len > max_size { return Err(Capacity(MessageTooLong)) }` runs BEFORE `self.in_buffer.reserve(len)` — i.e. the bound is enforced pre-allocation, not post-hoc. `check_max_size` is also applied cumulatively via `msg.extend(..., max_message_size)` across fragmented frames. So the sink at websocket.rs:292 only ever sees a `BytesMut` that upstream has already capped to ≤64 MiB.

2) The claim's contrast — "unlike BytesCodec::set_max_packet_length used on the raw-TCP path...which explicitly bounds preallocation" — is factually backwards. `grep -rn "set_max_packet_length"` across the entire rustdesk tree shows it is defined at bytes_codec.rs:40 but has ZERO call sites anywhere in the client, server, or hbb_common — it is dead API. At runtime `max_packet_length` stays at its `new()` default of `usize::MAX` (bytes_codec.rs:32), so the raw-TCP path has NO enforced maximum single-packet size at all (only the wire format's own 30-bit length field bounds it near ~1 GiB). The code comment the claim cites ("Bound speculative allocation from untrusted frame headers", bytes_codec.rs:5) actually documents a *different*, always-active mechanism — `MAX_PREALLOCATED_PAYLOAD_LEN` (256 KiB), which paces the first speculative `reserve()` regardless of the declared length, not `set_max_packet_length`. The claim conflates the two and misattributes the "hardening" to the dead function.

Net effect: the real asymmetry is the opposite of what's claimed. WS's untuned-but-upstream-enforced ceiling (16 MiB/frame, 64 MiB/message, checked pre-allocation) is materially TIGHTER than the raw-TCP custom protocol's practically-unbounded ceiling in this same codebase (set_max_packet_length never invoked). The one narrow, real residual issue on WS is that tungstenite's `read_frame` does a single eager `reserve(len)` for up to max_frame_size (16 MiB) triggered by a small header before any corresponding payload arrives — a bounded ~16 MiB-per-idle-connection speculative-allocation amplification, not an unbounded "alloc-bomb", and it is smaller in the worst case than what's already possible today on the raw-TCP path.

Trust-boundary/reachability part of the claim is fine: WsFramedStream is client-side code parsing frames from the rendezvous/relay server, matching documented trust boundary (2); `allow-websocket=Y` opt-in precondition is confirmed accurate (config.rs:2832-2837, `option2bool` treats "allow-*" keys as default-false unless "Y").
verdict.corrected_root_cause: WsFramedStream::try_connect passes `ws_config = None` (websocket.rs:98) so no app-tuned WebSocketConfig is applied; this resolves via tungstenite 0.26.2's `unwrap_or_default()` to its built-in defaults (max_message_size=64 MiB, max_frame_size=16 MiB), which ARE actively enforced pre-allocation in `read_frame` (`len > max_size` check before `reserve(len)`) and cumulatively across fragmented frames via `check_max_size`. The claimed contrast with a "hardened" raw-TCP BytesCodec path is incorrect: `BytesCodec::set_max_packet_length` (bytes_codec.rs:40) has zero call sites anywhere in the codebase and is dead code, so the raw-TCP path enforces no application max-packet-size at runtime (only the wire format's 30-bit length field bounds it to ~1 GiB, with only preallocation paced via the separate, always-on `MAX_PREALLOCATED_PAYLOAD_LEN` constant). The genuine, narrower residual gap is that tungstenite eagerly reserves up to the full declared frame length (≤16 MiB) from a minimal header before receiving the corresponding payload — a bounded per-idle-WS-connection amplification, smaller than what the un-tuned raw-TCP path already permits.
verdict.observed_mitigation: tungstenite 0.26.2 (Cargo.lock-pinned) enforces max_message_size=64MiB / max_frame_size=16MiB by default even when the caller passes None, checked before allocation (protocol/frame/mod.rs read_frame: `len > max_size` bails prior to `in_buffer.reserve(len)`); confirmed by fetching the actual crate source at tag v0.26.2. Separately, the "hardened" raw-TCP comparison in the claim cites `BytesCodec::set_max_packet_length`, which `grep -rn` across the whole repo shows is never called, so it provides no runtime protection to contrast against.
verdict.live_test: Not required to resolve the core question (settled via upstream source read), but for completeness: enable allow-websocket=Y, stand up a malicious ws:// endpoint impersonating hbbs, and send a single WS binary frame header declaring a 16 MiB (max_frame_size) payload while withholding the payload bytes on N concurrent client connections; expect RSS to grow by roughly N x up-to-16MiB and plateau there (bounded), never exceeding N x 64MiB even if payload is eventually completed — confirming the enforced ceiling and refuting any "unbounded" framing.

verdict.reason:
Read the full file. The claim is accurate line-for-line:
- fingerprint.rs:165-176 `get_key()`: computes `entropy = get_system_entropy()` (line 166), XORs it into `key` in a loop (171-174), then the final expression is `base` (line 175) — not `key`. Confirmed only one definition and one call site of `get_key()` (grep across libs/hbb_common/src/), so there's no alternate code path that uses the entropy-mixed key.
- Sha512Hasher::new() (line 306) stores this constant as `self.key`; finalize() (326-353) uses it in finalize_block() (71-89, a from-scratch AES-128 encrypt) to encrypt the last 16-32 bytes of the fingerprint input whenever the trailing buffer is non-empty — so the tail of every get_fingerprint() output is produced with a publicly known, invariant key.

All citations check out exactly as claimed.
- No mitigating check exists in this codebase: there's no second key source, no runtime feature-flag gating get_key(), and no server-side validation visible (backend is closed-source/out of repo), which the candidate already honestly discloses rather than assumes away.
Side observation that does NOT refute the claim but is worth carrying forward: get_system_entropy() (153-163) derives "entropy" from the current wall-clock nanosecond timestamp at call time, not any stable per-machine seed — so even a hypothetical fix that returned `key` instead of `base` would make the AES-obfuscated tail non-reproducible run-to-run (breaking device_id's use as a stable identifier), which is a separate design flaw in the entropy source, not evidence against the claimed bug. It also somewhat justifies keeping the "potential" severity capped at Medium rather than higher, since a naive fix doesn't obviously make this into a strong integrity mechanism.
I found no way to reject: the code does exactly what's claimed, the call chain to an externally-sent value is real and unconditional (no auth/feature gate), and the candidate's own severity/confidence (Low realized, Medium potential, 0.9 confidence) is already appropriately hedged around the fact that the only known consumer (api.rustdesk.com) is closed-source and not verifiable from this repo.

verdict.observed_mitigation: None found — get_key() is unconditional (no cfg/feature gate), single definition/single call site, and no server-side consumer code is present in this repo to validate device_id, so no mitigating layer is observable from source.

candidate.confidence_reason: Hash construction is directly readable and unambiguous (single SHA256 call, no iteration count); exploitability is gated on a separate file-exfiltration precondition not provable from this slice alone.

verdict.reason: compute_permanent_password_h1 (permanent_password.rs:23-34) is exactly SHA256(password||salt) with no iteration count and no KDF (verified: PBKDF2/scrypt/bcrypt/Argon2 do not appear anywhere in the repo -- rg -ni 'argon2|pbkdf2|bcrypt|scrypt' only hits an unrelated build.rs). The per-config salt (config.rs ensure_permanent_password_salt) prevents cross-install rainbow tables but adds zero per-guess cost, so an attacker holding h1 can brute-force at raw SHA-256 throughput (~10^9-10^10 H/s on a modern GPU). The full trace is verified against config.rs: set_permanent_password (1293) -> compute_permanent_password_storage_for_update (1325) calls compute_permanent_password_h1 then encode_permanent_password_encrypted_storage_from_h1 -> config.store() (718) persists it. entry_point/sink/trace lines all match the actual code. This makes the claim's severity framing conservative rather than overstated. This is a static, code-provable crypto-design fact (no live target/runtime needed to prove the hash construction lacks a work factor), so it does not need live validation to confirm the vulnerability itself -- only the compound exfiltration/local-key preconditions (already flagged by the candidate) affect real-world reachability, which the candidate correctly reflects via Medium actual / Critical potential severity and confidence 0.55.

verdict.observed_mitigation: None found that defeats the core claim. Salt (config.salt) is present and prevents cross-target rainbow tables but does not add per-guess cost. verdict.live_test: Not required to confirm the hashing weakness (provable statically), but to validate real-world reachability of the full chain: on a RustDesk client host, set a permanent password via the GUI/CLI, then read the config TOML (e.g. ~/.config/rustdesk/RustDesk2.toml on Linux, %APPDATA%/RustDesk/config/RustDesk2.toml on Windows) as the same OS user (or as root/service) and extract the 'password' and 'salt' fields. Expected safe/non-vulnerable result would instead show a stored hash formatted as Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt (e.g. '$argon2id$...'), which is not what encode_permanent_password_storage_from_h1 produces.

candidate.title: Preset permanent-password comparison falls back to non-constant-time string equality when no salt is configured
candidate.root_cause: preset_permanent_password_storage_matches_plain in config/permanent_password.rs does not use a constant-time comparison when salt is empty (`return storage == input;`), allowing a timing side channel to recover the preset/admin permanent password byte-by-byte via repeated password-change attempts.
candidate.entry_point: Config::set_permanent_password(password) in config.rs:1293, which calls preset_permanent_password_storage_matches_plain(&preset_storage, &preset_salt, password) with caller-supplied `password` — reachable by any local process able to invoke the password-change path, including the cross-user shared '_service' IPC channel noted in config.rs.
candidate.sink: `storage == input` at permanent_password.rs:168 — a Rust &str equality that short-circuits on the first mismatching byte, not constant-time (unlike constant_time_eq_32 used for the salted/hashed branch just below it).
candidate.trace: Config::set_permanent_password (config.rs:1293) -> preset_permanent_password_storage_matches_plain (permanent_password.rs:159) -> early-return `storage == input` (permanent_password.rs:168) when preset_salt.is_empty().
candidate.attack: For a deployment configured with a legacy/no-salt HARD_SETTINGS preset password, a local attacker with access to the password-change IPC path repeatedly submits guessed passwords and measures response timing to recover the organization's preset password one byte at a time, since comparison exits as soon as a byte differs.
candidate.preconditions: default config: no — only exercised when the preset password's salt is empty (legacy/unsalted preset password deployment); requires local ability to invoke the password-change path repeatedly with attacker-controlled timing measurement.
candidate.confidence_reason: Code path is unambiguous and directly readable; real-world exploitability depends on IPC access control and timing-measurement precision not visible in this two-file slice.

verdict.reason:
Re-read permanent_password.rs in full: the code fact is real — preset_permanent_password_storage_matches_plain() at line 167-168 does `return storage == input;` (a non-constant-time &str compare) whenever preset_salt is empty, vs. constant_time_eq_32() on the salted/hashed branch just below. That part of the claim holds.

But the claim's reachability/entry-point description is factually wrong and I can cite the exact mitigating code. The claim asserts this is reachable "including the cross-user shared '_service' IPC channel noted in config.rs." I traced the actual call chain: Config::set_permanent_password (config.rs:1293) is only invoked from the IPC handler's `Data::Config(("permanent-password", Some(value)))` arm (src/ipc.rs:886-893). That arm is reached from the generic `handle()` dispatcher — but for the `_service` postfix specifically, src/ipc.rs:525-540 installs an explicit allowlist: `if postfix == crate::POSTFIX_SERVICE { if matches!(&data, Data::SyncConfig(_)) { handle(...) } else { ...break } }` — i.e. on the `_service` channel, ONLY `Data::SyncConfig` messages reach `handle()`; a `Data::Config` message (which is what carries "permanent-password") is explicitly rejected and the connection is torn down. So the timing-vulnerable comparison is provably NOT reachable via `_service` at all.

The code path that actually IS reachable is the main IPC channel (postfix ""), confirmed at src/ipc.rs:1610 (`connect(ms_timeout, "")` inside set_permanent_password_with_ack_async). That listener's socket is created with mode 0o0600 (src/ipc.rs:625-631: `let socket_mode = if config::is_service_ipc_postfix(postfix) { 0o0666 } else { 0o0600 };` and `is_service_ipc_postfix` only matches `_service`/`_uinput_*`, config.rs:128-135). A 0600 Unix-socket file is connectable only by the owning UID or root — not "any local process," not cross-user.

So the entry-point claim overstates reachability: the vulnerable comparison is exercisable only by a process already running as the same OS user (or root) as the RustDesk service, via the owner-only main IPC socket — never via the cross-user `_service` channel, which is code-gated against it.</reason>

That socket is created with mode 0o0600 (src/ipc.rs:613-631), so only a process running as the same OS user as the RustDesk daemon (or root) can connect and drive repeated guesses. The cross-user `_service` IPC channel cannot reach this function: src/ipc.rs:525-540 hard-filters that channel to `Data::SyncConfig` messages only, rejecting and closing on any `Data::Config` (the message kind that carries "permanent-password"). Exploitation additionally requires a non-default deployment where the preset/hard-settings password was configured without a salt (plaintext preset password) and password-change is not disabled (Config::is_disable_change_permanent_password() == false).</corrected_root_cause>
<parameter name="corrected_severity">Low
verdict.observed_mitigation: src/ipc.rs:525-540 — explicit SyncConfig-only allowlist on the `_service` postfix channel blocks Data::Config("permanent-password", ...) from ever reaching Config::set_permanent_password on that cross-user channel. src/ipc.rs:613-631 — non-service IPC sockets (including the postfix "" main channel actually used by set_permanent_password_with_ack_async, ipc.rs:1610) are created with mode 0o0600, restricting connection to the owning UID/root, not "any local process."

candidate.title: Default temporary (one-time) password has only ~20-30 bits of entropy
candidate.root_cause: temporary_password_length in password_security.rs defaults to 6 characters, and Config::get_auto_password_with_chars (config.rs:1083) draws from a small alphabet (10 digits or ~31 alnum chars), so the default one-time password protecting incoming P2P connections has only ~20-30 bits of entropy.
candidate.entry_point: A remote peer initiating a P2P connection to this host's RustDesk ID via hbbs/hbbr (pre-auth trust boundary) and supplying guessed temporary-password values during the connection handshake's password-verification step.
candidate.sink: TEMPORARY_PASSWORD static (password_security.rs:6), generated by get_auto_password()/update_temporary_password() (password_security.rs:23-35) and later compared during connection authentication (comparison logic itself lives outside this slice, but the weak secret is minted here).
candidate.trace: get_auto_password (password_security.rs:23) -> Config::get_auto_password/get_auto_numeric_password (config.rs:1075-1081, length = temporary_password_length()=6 by default, password_security.rs:53-62) -> Config::get_auto_password_with_chars (config.rs:1083) -> TEMPORARY_PASSWORD -> used by connection auth (outside this slice).
candidate.attack: Default RustDesk config uses the 'use-both-passwords' verification method with the temporary password at its default 6-digit/6-char length. An internet attacker who has hole-punched or relayed a connection to the victim's known numeric ID can attempt online guesses of the 6-character/6-digit temporary password; absent strong rate-limiting elsewhere in the stack, this is a tractable brute force to gain full remote-control access before the password auto-rotates.
candidate.preconditions: default config: yes (6-char/6-digit is the out-of-box default; 8/10-digit stronger options exist but are opt-in); requires temporary-password verification enabled (default) and the attacker to know/guess the victim's numeric ID.
candidate.confidence_reason: Entropy calculation is directly derivable from the visible alphabet/length constants; whether hbbs/hbbr or the client enforces attempt rate-limiting or lockout is outside this two-file slice and materially changes real-world risk.

verdict.reason: The entropy math in password_security.rs is accurate as far as it goes (get_auto_password_with_chars, config.rs:1083-1088: length=temporary_password_length()=6 by default (password_security.rs:53-62), drawn from CHARS = 32-char alnum alphabet (config.rs:115-118) unless the non-default 'allow-numeric-one-time-password' option is set, which starts with 'allow-' so option2bool defaults it to false/off (config.rs:2832-2837) — i.e. the DEFAULT temp password is ~30 bits (32^6), not the ~20-bit numeric case). But the claim's central exploitability assertion — 'absent strong rate-limiting elsewhere in the stack, this is a tractable brute force' — is directly refuted by code in the very connection-auth sink the claim flagged as unobserved. src/server/connection.rs implements two independent, default-on, unconditional brute-force mitigations that run for every non-empty-password login attempt, before/around validate_password: (1) per-IP (and per-IPv6-prefix) throttling — max 6 wrong attempts/minute and a PERMANENT lockout after 30 lifetime wrong attempts per source IP (connection.rs:4094-4127, :4001-4034), checked via check_failure() BEFORE validate_password runs (connection.rs:2723-2726) so a throttled/locked IP never even reaches the password comparison; and (2) a global (not per-IP) consecutive-failure counter specific to the temporary password (check_update_temporary_password, connection.rs:2244-2294, wired in at :2306 success-reset and :2729 failure-increment) that force-rotates the ENTIRE temporary password to a fresh independent random value after only 10 consecutive wrong guesses server-wide, regardless of how many distinct source IPs are used. Combined, a determined attacker's maximum lifetime guesses against a single RustDesk server are bounded by roughly 30 x (number of distinct attacker-controlled source IPs), and even a large (~100k-node) botnet nets only ~3,000,000 total guesses against a 32^6≈1.07e9 keyspace — well under 1% success probability. This is a real, present, default-active mitigation directly readable in the same repo, not an assumed/unseen layer, so it satisfies the 'mitigating check is PRESENT in code you can read' refutation criterion. The underlying weak-secret design point (6-char default, and a much weaker opt-in numeric-only 6-digit mode with ~10^6 keyspace where a very large distributed botnet could plausibly get meaningful hit probability despite the same mitigations) is a legitimate defense-in-depth concern, so this is 'corrected' rather than fully rejected — but the claimed High/Critical severity and the 'tractable brute force' framing for the DEFAULT configuration are not supported once the observed rate-limiting/rotation logic is accounted for.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: temporary_password_length() defaults to 6 (password_security.rs:53-62) and Config::get_auto_password_with_chars draws from a 32-char alnum alphabet by default (config.rs:113-118,1075-1088), giving ~30 bits of entropy for the default temp password (or ~19.93 bits if the non-default numeric-only option is opted into). However, src/server/connection.rs enforces default-on, unconditional brute-force mitigation that the original claim did not account for: per-IP throttling (6 wrong attempts/min) plus a permanent per-IP lifetime lockout after 30 wrong attempts (connection.rs:4094-4127), checked before password validation (connection.rs:2723-2726), and a separate global consecutive-failure counter that auto-rotates the entire temporary password after just 10 consecutive wrong guesses server-wide (connection.rs:2244-2294). verdict.observed_mitigation: src/server/connection.rs: check_failure()/check_failure_with_scope() (called at connection.rs:2723, definition ~4036-4128) enforce per-IP throttling (max 6 wrong attempts/minute, connection.rs:4113-4123) and a permanent per-IP lifetime lockout after 30 wrong attempts (connection.rs:4102-4112), plus IPv6-prefix-scoped equivalents (connection.rs:4001-4034) — all evaluated BEFORE validate_password() runs, so a throttled/locked-out IP never reaches the password comparison. verdict.live_test: Against a lab RustDesk host with default settings (verification-method unset -> use-both-passwords, temporary-password-length unset -> 6, allow-numeric-one-time-password unset -> alnum), send >6 LoginRequest messages with wrong temporary passwords from one source IP within 60s: expect the 7th+ attempt in that minute to receive login_error 'Please try 1 minute later' (connection.rs:4114) instead of 'Wrong Password' -- confirms per-IP throttle is live. Separately, send exactly 10 consecutive wrong-password LoginRequests (can be spread across several source IPs to avoid the per-IP throttle) and then attempt the previously-valid temp password from `rustdesk --get-conf` / config storage on the target: expect authentication to FAIL because the password value has changed (rotated) -- confirms the global 10-consecutive-failure auto-rotation in check_update_temporary_password is live. If either behavior is absent (throttle message never appears after 6 fails/min, or old password still works after 10 consecutive fails), the mitigation is not actually active at runtime and the original High/Critical severity should be reinstated.

verdict.reason:
The core mechanism is real and directly verifiable: `is_encrypted()` (password_security.rs:107-115) classifies any byte string as "already encrypted" purely from shape — starts with ASCII "00", the remainder is valid base64, decoded length >= secretbox::MACBYTES (16) — without ever attempting to actually open the secretbox. `encrypt_str_or_original`/`encrypt_vec_or_original` (lines 117-131, 160-176) short-circuit on that heuristic and `return s.to_owned()`/`v.to_owned()` verbatim, skipping `symmetric_crypt(..., true)` entirely. This is not a subtle oversight — the file's own comment (lines 100-106, "We intentionally avoid trying to decrypt here because key mismatch would cause false negatives") and its own test suite (test_is_encrypted lines 421-425, and the `exact_mac`/`00YWJjZA==` cases in the main test at lines 336-361) explicitly construct and assert this exact plaintext-classified-as-ciphertext collision as expected behavior — RustDesk devs knowingly accepted this heuristic trade-off.

However, the claim's entry_point list over-scopes reachability, which I can point to directly:
1. `trusted_devices` is NOT a viable entry point. Its value is always `serde_json::to_string(&trusted_devices)` (config.rs:1623), a JSON array that always starts with '[', never with the literal bytes "00" — `is_encrypted`'s line-108 check (`!v.starts_with(b"00")`) makes it unconditionally false for this field. This claimed entry point is definitively unreachable.
2. `PeerConfig.password` is also a weak/impractical entry point in practice: tracing client.rs:3505-3527, the bytes written to `config.password` are `SHA256(secret || hash.salt)` — a uniformly-distributed 32-byte digest, not literal attacker-chosen text. Landing this specific "00"-prefix + valid-base64 + ≥16-byte-decode shape by chance is astronomically improbable, and SHA256 preimage resistance means an attacker cannot simply choose an input to engineer the output shape (unlike the claim's framing of "attacker-chosen bytes").

The genuinely reachable, directly attacker/operator-controllable entry points are the free-text option fields actually confirmed via config.rs:1749-1752 (`rdp_password`, `os-username`, `os-password`, set as literal UI/IPC strings — flutter_ffi.rs/ui_interface.rs confirm these are raw user-supplied strings) and `Config2.socks.password` / `Config2.unlock_pin` (config.rs:526-531, 1583-1593), which are set locally via UI/IPC (ipc.rs:905,1631; flutter_ffi.rs:2162) — not remotely attacker-reachable in these two files, so realistic triggering requires either (a) a low-probability natural collision with a base64-charset-generated credential, or (b) a local user/admin/address-book-preset deliberately supplying a value in this shape (self-inflicted or trusted-source-supplied, not a remote-attacker-forged secret). No remote/network attacker path to force *someone else's* independently-chosen secret into this shape was found in these files.

Given the underlying "protection" being bypassed is itself weak (the secretbox key is derived locally and deterministically from the machine's own UUID/keypair — crate::get_uuid(), password_security.rs:216-219 — so it only obstructs naive file-scraping, not a co-resident attacker capable of running the same decrypt routine), and 2 of 6 claimed entry points are inaccurate/overclaimed, Medium is too high; Low is the accurate severity for a genuine but narrow-blast-radius, largely self-inflicted or low-probability-collision at-rest-obfuscation bypass.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: encrypt_str_or_original/encrypt_vec_or_original (password_security.rs:117-131,160-176) use a purely shape-based heuristic (is_encrypted, lines 107-115: "00" prefix + valid base64 + decoded length >= MACBYTES) to detect already-encrypted values and skip re-encryption. This is a deliberate, developer-acknowledged and test-covered trade-off (comment lines 100-106; tests lines 336-361, 421-425), not an unknown bug. It is genuinely reachable only via the free-text local option fields that are directly settable to literal attacker/operator-chosen strings — `options['rdp_password'|'os-username'|'os-password']` (config.rs:1749-1752) and `Config2.socks.password`/`Config2.unlock_pin` (config.rs:526-531,1583-1593), all set via local UI/IPC, not remote network input in the files reviewed. `trusted_devices` is unreachable (its JSON payload always starts with '[', never "00" — password_security.rs:108, config.rs:1623). `PeerConfig.password` is a SHA256 digest (client.rs:3505-3527), not literal attacker text, so hitting the collision shape there is astronomically improbable and not attacker-engineerable via preimage choice.
verdict.observed_mitigation: None present in code that prevents the collision itself (no HMAC/random-marker distinguishing real ciphertext from shape-alike plaintext) — the collision is real and directly demonstrable. What limits real-world impact is scope: the vulnerable fields with genuinely attacker/operator-controllable literal string content (rdp_password/os-username/os-password/socks.password/unlock_pin) are all local-UI/IPC-set only (ipc.rs:905,1631,1818; flutter_ffi.rs:2162) with no remote-network setter found in these files, and the field the claim leans on most (PeerConfig.password) is SHA256-hash-derived (client.rs:3505-3527), not literal text, making that specific vector practically unreachable. trusted_devices is structurally unreachable because its JSON serialization can never start with the required "00" prefix (config.rs:1623 vs. password_security.rs:108).
verdict.live_test: Not required for verdict (corrected, provable from static artifacts), but for empirical confirmation: on a build with RustDesk client running, set an RDP-forward saved credential via UI to the literal string `00AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA==` (i.e. "00" + base64 of 16 zero bytes) for a peer's `os-password`/`rdp_password` option, trigger a config store (e.g. connect/disconnect the RDP-tunnel session so PeerConfig::store_ runs), then read the peer's `.toml` file under the RustDesk config dir. Vulnerable: the option value is stored byte-identical to `00AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA==` (no re-encryption, decodes back to the literal string, not a FORMAT_V1-prefixed secretbox blob). Safe/patched: the stored value differs from the input (freshly secretbox-sealed each store, decoding to `FORMAT_V1 || nonce || ciphertext`, and `symmetric_crypt` on it round-trips to the original secret rather than to `AAAA...` zero bytes).

candidate.title: Secrets longer than ENCRYPT_MAX_LEN are silently reduced to an empty string/vector instead of failing
candidate.root_cause: encrypt_str_or_original/encrypt_vec_or_original silently return an empty String/Vec when the plaintext exceeds max_len (ENCRYPT_MAX_LEN=128) instead of returning an error or refusing the store, so an over-length secret (e.g. a long RDP/OS password) is silently persisted as an empty value with no error signal.
candidate.entry_point: Any secret value >128 bytes/chars assigned to PeerConfig.password/options or Config2 socks.password/unlock_pin/trusted_devices, whether locally entered or synced from an external source.
candidate.sink: `return String::default();` (password_security.rs:123) / `return vec![];` (password_security.rs:166) — persisted to disk in place of the real secret.
candidate.trace: PeerConfig::store_ / Config2::store (config.rs) -> encrypt_str_or_original|encrypt_vec_or_original -> length check fails -> empty value silently written to the .toml file, replacing the real secret.
candidate.attack: A caller that stores a >128-byte credential (a long generated RDP/OS password, or an attacker-influenced synced credential field) ends up with an empty string persisted; if any downstream logic treats an empty stored credential as 'no password required,' this silently weakens protection for that peer/config entry instead of surfacing a clear failure.
candidate.preconditions: default config: yes (no gating on the length check); actual security impact depends on unseen downstream handling of an empty stored credential.
candidate.confidence_reason: The truncation-to-empty is directly visible in code, but the entry point is weakly attacker-controlled from within these two files (most callers are local-user-supplied), and the downstream consequence of an empty value is not verifiable in this slice.

verdict.reason: The mechanical claim is accurate: password_security.rs:122-123 (encrypt_str_or_original) and :165-166 (encrypt_vec_or_original) do silently return an empty String/Vec when the plaintext exceeds max_len, with no error returned/logged to the caller — confirmed by reading the file. This is inconsistent with the sibling caller at libs/hbb_common/src/config.rs:1624-1628 (set_trusted_devices), which explicitly checks the length first and log::error!()s + bails before calling encrypt_str_or_original, so trusted_devices never hits the silent-empty path. The password/options callers (PeerConfig::store_ at config.rs:1745-1753, Config2::store at config.rs:517-533) have no such pre-check, so the truncation-to-empty is real and unguarded there. However, the claim's core security worry — "if any downstream logic treats an empty stored credential as no password required, this silently weakens protection" — is refuted by every concrete downstream consumer I could find in this repo, and no attacker-controlled entry point was found: (1) src/client.rs:1911-1920 should_auto_login() explicitly gates on `!p.is_empty()` for the os-password field, so a truncated-to-empty password fails closed (no auto-login) rather than being treated as "no password needed". (2) src/client.rs:3531-3536 + 3568-3571: an empty PeerConfig.password falls through to the standard "login without password, the remote side can click accept" flow — the normal RustDesk no-saved-password UX that still requires interactive approval on the remote peer, not an authentication bypass. (3) flutter/lib/desktop/pages/desktop_setting_page.dart:2882-2889: an empty unlock_pin routes to callMainCheckSuperUserPermission() (an OS-level check) instead of skipping authorization entirely — a substituted control, not an absence of one. Separately, none of the affected fields (PeerConfig.password/options['os-username'|'os-password'|'rdp_password'], Config2.socks.password, Config2.unlock_pin) is ever populated from a network-attacker-controlled source in this codebase: grep shows they are set only via local GUI dialogs / IPC / CLI args (src/ui_session_interface.rs, src/client.rs set_option, src/ipc.rs, src/core_main.rs, src/flutter_ffi.rs) — none of the four defined RustDesk trust boundaries (hbbs/hbbr pre-auth, rendezvous→client, peer→controlled host, host→controller) feeds these fields. The permanent-password path (libs/hbb_common/src/config/permanent_password.rs:74-77 encrypt_permanent_password_storage) is also unaffected in practice because it encrypts a fixed-size SHA-256 hash-encoded storage string (~44 chars), never the raw arbitrary-length password, so a long login password can't trigger the truncation there. Net: real bug (silent credential data loss with no error surfaced — a robustness/logging defect worth fixing), but it is self-inflicted by the local operator entering an oversized secret, not attacker-reachable, and every observed downstream consumer fails closed rather than granting unauthorized access. The claim's potential_severity: Medium / needs-live-validation escalation is not supported once the actual downstream consumers are read — they're in this same repo, not an unseen layer.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: encrypt_str_or_original/encrypt_vec_or_original (password_security.rs:117-131, 160-176) silently discard secrets longer than max_len (returning empty String/Vec) with no error path, unlike the sibling trusted_devices caller which pre-checks length and logs+bails (config.rs:1624-1628). This causes silent loss of any locally-entered PeerConfig.password/os-username/os-password/rdp_password or Config2.socks.password/unlock_pin longer than 128 chars. It is a data-integrity/UX robustness defect, not a security bypass: all affected fields are populated only via local GUI/IPC/CLI input (no attacker-controlled entry point observed across any RustDesk trust boundary), and the concrete downstream consumers found (should_auto_login at client.rs:1911-1920, connection-password fallback at client.rs:3531-3571, unlock-pin check at desktop_setting_page.dart:2882-2889) all treat the resulting empty value as fail-closed (require re-entry, remote click-accept, or a substituted OS-level check) rather than as "no credential required".
verdict.observed_mitigation: src/client.rs:1911-1920 should_auto_login() checks `!p.is_empty()` before using os-password for auto-login (fails closed on truncated-to-empty). src/client.rs:3531-3536,3568-3571: empty PeerConfig.password routes to the standard "remote side can click accept" interactive-approval flow, not an unconditional login. flutter/lib/desktop/pages/desktop_setting_page.dart:2882-2889: empty unlock_pin substitutes callMainCheckSuperUserPermission() (OS-level check) rather than skipping authorization. libs/hbb_common/src/config.rs:1624-1628 shows the codebase's own established pattern (pre-check + log::error! + bail) that the password-path callers simply omit — a code-quality inconsistency, not evidence the omission is exploitable.
verdict.live_test: Not required — the relevant downstream logic (should_auto_login, connection-password fallback, unlock-pin check) is present in this repo and was read directly; all three fail closed on an empty value rather than granting access.

candidate.title: Unauthenticated ConfigureUpdate lets rendezvous server permanently hijack the client's trust anchor

candidate.sink: libs/hbb_common/src/config.rs Config::set_option()/Config::set_serial() (lines ~1010, ~1259) persist the values to disk via config.store(); Config::get_rendezvous_servers() (line 936) is then polled by RendezvousMediator::start_all()'s connect loop to choose which host(s) to dial for every future register_peer/register_pk/PunchHole/RequestRelay/FetchLocalAddr exchange.
candidate.trace: 1) rendezvous_mediator.rs:270/458 Message::parse_from_bytes parses attacker-controlled bytes -> 2) rendezvous_mediator.rs:407 handle_resp matches ConfigureUpdate(cu) -> 3) rendezvous_mediator.rs:409-413 unconditionally Config::set_option("rendezvous-servers", cu.rendezvous_servers.join(",")) then Config::set_serial(cu.serial) -> 4) config.rs:1010-1017 set_serial stores serial with no bound/signature check -> 5) config.rs:936-961 get_rendezvous_servers() re-evaluates serial_obsolute = CONFIG2.serial > SERIAL (now true) and returns the attacker's list -> 6) rendezvous_mediator.rs:414-416 detects the list changed and calls Self::restart() -> 7) rendezvous_mediator.rs:153-183 start_all()'s loop re-reads Config::get_rendezvous_servers() next iteration and dials the attacker host for every subsequent protocol exchange, including after process restart since the value was persisted to disk.
candidate.attack: Attacker who is (or MITMs) the client's configured rendezvous server, or on the UDP transport (which carries zero transport-level crypto/authentication) any network attacker able to spoof/inject one UDP datagram to the client, sends RendezvousMessage{ConfigureUpdate{rendezvous_servers:["evil.attacker.tld"], serial: 2147483647}}. Verified the default-config precondition is accurate, not an unverified assumption: EXE_RENDEZVOUS_SERVER is only ever written in src/platform/windows.rs:2165 for Windows-license builds; grep shows PROD_RENDEZVOUS_SERVER is never written anywhere in this codebase (read-only, empty by default); custom-rendezvous-server is an operator-set option, empty by default. So a stock/default client (non-Windows-license) has all three short-circuits empty, meaning get_rendezvous_servers() reaches the vulnerable serial-gated branch on every call — the claim's \"default config: yes\" is directly verifiable, not assumed. Persistence via config.store() inside set_option/set_serial (confirmed pattern used throughout config.rs, e.g. set_id at :988-995) means the hijack survives process/app restart, matching the claim's durability assertion. No mitigating check anywhere in the cited call path — no signature over ConfigUpdate, no allow-list of hosts, no confirmation prompt, no rate limit specific to this message type. This is not a case of assuming an unseen layer is secure; every claimed step (parse -> handle_resp match arm -> set_option -> set_serial -> gate re-evaluation -> restart -> next connect loop dials new host) is directly readable and was independently traced through rendezvous_mediator.rs, config.rs, and rendezvous.proto.

candidate.title: Server-controlled RequestRelay.secure=false skips the NaCl peer-identity handshake for relay-mediated inbound connections

candidate.entry_point: RequestRelay message (relay_server: string, secure: bool, socket_addr: bytes, uuid: string) pushed unsolicited by the rendezvous server; dispatched in handle_resp (rendezvous_mediator.rs:393-398) to handle_request_relay.
candidate.sink: server.rs create_tcp_connection() (~line 206): `if secure && ...` gates the entire sign+box identity handshake block; when secure==false that block is skipped and Connection::start(addr, stream, id, ..., meta) (line 269) is invoked directly on the raw, unauthenticated stream.
candidate.trace: 1) rendezvous_mediator.rs:393-398 handle_resp dispatches RequestRelay(rr) -> 2) rendezvous_mediator.rs:495-519 handle_request_relay reads rr.relay_server/rr.secure off the wire, calls create_relay(..., rr.secure, false, ...) -> 3) rendezvous_mediator.rs:521-566 create_relay calls crate::create_relay_connection(server, relay_server, uuid, peer_addr, secure, ...) -> 4) server.rs:285-327 create_relay_connection/create_relay_connection_ dials connect_tcp(check_port(relay_server, RELAY_PORT)) -> 5) server.rs:336 create_tcp_connection(server, stream, peer_addr, secure, meta) -> 6) server.rs:206-255 NaCl handshake block skipped because secure==false -> 7) server.rs:269 Connection::start() begins treating the raw stream as an inbound remote-control session.
candidate.attack: Malicious/MITM rendezvous server sends RequestRelay{relay_server:"attacker.example:6000", secure:false, socket_addr:<arbitrary AddrMangle bytes>, uuid:"x"} to a running client with no corresponding request from any real peer. Observed result: the client dials out to attacker.example:6000, skips the NaCl identity-binding handshake, and hands the resulting stream straight to Connection::start() as an inbound session — removing the cryptographic peer-identity pinning that trusted-device/whitelist/peer-ID-display features rely on, and forcing an attacker-directed outbound connection to boot.
candidate.preconditions: default config: yes for the dial-out + handshake-skip mechanics (no client setting gates this branch). Depth of session takeover (silent full control vs. still-gated login prompt) depends on the device's local login policy (permanent/weak password, or any ID-based trust list that assumed the now-missing NaCl binding) — that downstream piece is outside this file and needs live validation.
candidate.confidence_reason: The attacker-controlled secure/relay_server fields and the resulting skip of the NaCl handshake plus raw-stream handoff to Connection::start are directly confirmed by reading both rendezvous_mediator.rs and server.rs; full unauthenticated-takeover depth depends on Connection::start's internal login/password logic, not reviewed in this slice.

verdict.reason: The core code-level mechanism is confirmed exactly as claimed: rendezvous_mediator.rs:393-399 dispatches an unsolicited server-pushed RequestRelay message to handle_request_relay (line 495), which passes rr.secure verbatim into create_relay (line 508-518, positional arg 5 = secure), which passes it unchanged into crate::create_relay_connection (line 557-566) -> server.rs create_relay_connection_ (314-338) -> create_tcp_connection(..., secure, ...) (line 336). In create_tcp_connection, `if secure && pk.len()==... && sk.len()==...` (server.rs:206) gates the ENTIRE NaCl sign+box handshake block (206-255); when secure==false that block is skipped entirely and the code falls straight through to `Connection::start(addr, stream, id, ..., meta)` (line 269) on the raw, un-key-set stream. No validation of rr.secure or rr.relay_server exists anywhere in the chain; the 100ms LAST_RELAY_MSG dedup (line 497-502) is trivially bypassed by varying the encoded address or waiting. This is a real, provable transport-security downgrade: skipping the block means stream.set_key() is never called, so the resulting session has neither cryptographic peer-identity binding nor encryption for that leg — enabling a hostile/MITM rendezvous server (or, since start_udp's default UDP registration path shows no server-authenticity check on inbound datagrams, potentially even a UDP source-spoofer) to force the client to dial an attacker-chosen relay_server and hand it a bare unauthenticated/unencrypted stream. So the claim's "auth-bypass" framing / unconditional Critical severity is not supported by the code actually reachable from these files: an attacker who exploits secure=false still cannot control the session without separately defeating the device's password (or exploiting a downstream trust-list logic not present in these files). verdict.observed_mitigation: Connection::start (connection.rs:452-591) initializes authorized=false and only sets it true after an independent password/2FA challenge-response succeeds (verify_h1/validate_password_plain/validate_password_storage, connection.rs:2196-2242; 2FA gate at 1619-1657).
