verdict.live_test: Stand up a mock/MITM rendezvous UDP endpoint (or intercept the real one) and, without any prior legitimate PunchHole exchange, send the target client a crafted RequestRelay{relay_server:"<tester-host>:6000", secure:false, socket_addr:<any AddrMangle-encoded bytes>, uuid:"x"}. On <tester-host>:6000 run a raw TCP listener that first reads the RelayResponse frame the client sends, then captures whatever the client sends next. Vulnerable/expected-per-claim result: client dials tester-host:6000 and the very next protobuf frame from the client is NOT a SignedId message (i.e., no sign::sign()-wrapped IdPk) — it goes straight into the Connection::start message loop (first frame accepted is something the LoginRequest handler processes), and no stream.set_key() ever occurs (traffic stays in cleartext/unencrypted protobuf framing, verifiable by capturing raw bytes and confirming they parse directly as protobuf rather than being NaCl-boxed). Control/patched-expected result: with secure:true in the same crafted message, the client's first frame is a SignedId message and the listener must reply with a valid PublicKey message within CONNECT_TIMEOUT or the connection is torn down before reaching the login stage. Separately confirm the retained barrier: without knowing/guessing the target's configured password, the tester's subsequent LoginRequest is rejected (authorized stays false, no control granted) in both the secure=false and secure=true cases — demonstrating the bug removes transport encryption/identity-binding but not the password gate.

candidate.title: relay_server field from PunchHole/FetchLocalAddr/RequestRelay drives an unvalidated outbound TCP connect (SSRF-style network-reach primitive)
candidate.root_cause: get_relay_server() falls back to the server-supplied relay_server string whenever the local "relay-server" option is unset (the out-of-box default), and none of the PunchHole, FetchLocalAddr, or RequestRelay handlers validate that string against any allow-list before it becomes the TCP dial target in create_relay_connection_, letting the rendezvous server steer the client's outbound relay connection to an arbitrary attacker-chosen host:port.
candidate.entry_point: relay_server field of PunchHole, FetchLocalAddr, or RequestRelay messages sent by the rendezvous server.
candidate.sink: server.rs create_relay_connection_(): socket_client::connect_tcp(ipv4_to_ipv6(crate::check_port(relay_server, RELAY_PORT), ipv4), CONNECT_TIMEOUT) — the attacker string is used directly as the connect target with no host/IP allow-list, so loopback, RFC1918, and link-local metadata addresses are all permitted.
candidate.trace: 1) rendezvous_mediator.rs:669 (handle_punch_hole) / 579 (handle_intranet) self.get_relay_server(ph.relay_server / fla.relay_server) returns the server-provided string unchanged when Config option "relay-server" is empty -> 2) rendezvous_mediator.rs:677-688 / 606-616 create_relay(..., relay_server, ...) -> 3) rendezvous_mediator.rs:556-566 crate::create_relay_connection(server, relay_server, ...) -> 4) server.rs:314-327 create_relay_connection_ dials connect_tcp(check_port(relay_server, RELAY_PORT)) against the attacker-chosen host:port and immediately sends a RequestRelay preamble.
candidate.attack: Malicious/MITM rendezvous server answers a normal PunchHole or FetchLocalAddr negotiation (triggered by any legitimate inbound-connection attempt) with relay_server="169.254.169.254:80" or an internal RFC1918 host:port instead of a real hbbr relay address. Observed result: the victim client, from its own network position, opens a TCP connection to that address and writes a short protobuf preamble to it — usable to probe/fingerprint internal or loopback services reachable from the victim host, and to make the client originate attacker-chosen connections.
candidate.preconditions: default config: yes — reachable whenever the local "relay-server" option is unset (the default), during any PunchHole/FetchLocalAddr negotiation for an inbound connection or an unsolicited RequestRelay.
candidate.confidence_reason: The connect-anywhere dial-out mechanics and absence of any allow-list are fully confirmed in source across rendezvous_mediator.rs and server.rs; real-world impact is environment-dependent on what is reachable from the victim's network position.

verdict.reason: Full trace verified directly in source, no mitigation found. get_relay_server() (rendezvous_mediator.rs:825-834) returns Config::get_option("relay-server") which is empty by default (DEFAULT_SETTINGS is an empty HashMap, config.rs:76; no code path pre-populates "relay-server" except an opt-in license-deploy flow in core_main.rs:513 and unit tests in websocket.rs), so by default it falls through to `provided_by_rendezvous_server` (the server/attacker-controlled field). handle_punch_hole (line 669) and handle_intranet (line 579) both call get_relay_server() with ph.relay_server / fla.relay_server; handle_request_relay (lines 495-519) is even more direct — it passes rr.relay_server straight into create_relay() without going through get_relay_server() at all, unconditionally trusting the server-supplied string regardless of local config (this strengthens, not weakens, the claim). create_relay() (line 521-568) forwards relay_server unchanged into crate::create_relay_connection() (line 557-566), which calls server.rs create_relay_connection_() (lines 314-338): `socket_client::connect_tcp(socket_client::ipv4_to_ipv6(crate::check_port(relay_server, RELAY_PORT), ipv4), CONNECT_TIMEOUT)` — verified this exact call chain, matching the claim's sink description verbatim. check_port() (common.rs:904-906 -> socket_client.rs:16-28) only normalizes host:port formatting — no host/IP validation, no allow-list. connect_tcp/connect_tcp_local (socket_client.rs:127-170+) resolve and dial the target with zero restriction on loopback/RFC1918/link-local. Immediately after connecting, create_relay_connection_ sends a RequestRelay preamble containing the license key and uuid (server.rs:328-335), exactly as claimed. Reachability is confirmed and found to be even broader than stated: default transport is UDP (rendezvous_mediator.rs:484-492, chosen unless debug+TEST_TCP/proxy/ws/udp-disabled), and the UDP receive loop (line 267-274) parses `Message::parse_from_bytes(&bytes)` directly from any received UDP datagram and discards the source address entirely (`Some(Ok((bytes, _)))`) — there is no verification that the packet originated from the configured rendezvous server, and no signature/auth field exists on PunchHole/RequestRelay/FetchLocalAddr in rendezvous.proto. So this is exploitable not just by a malicious/MITM rendezvous server but by any host able to send a spoofed/arbitrary UDP packet to the client's rendezvous port — a strictly stronger reachability than claimed, not weaker. No allow-list, cert pinning of the relay target, or private-IP filter was found anywhere in the traced path. The claim's Medium (confirmed) / High (potential) severity framing for an SSRF-style outbound-dial primitive is technically accurate and not inflated to RCE.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: Same as claimed, with one addition: handle_request_relay() (rendezvous_mediator.rs:495-519) does not even call get_relay_server() — it passes the server-supplied RequestRelay.relay_server straight into create_relay() unconditionally, regardless of the local "relay-server" config option. So the RequestRelay entry point is unconditionally attacker-steerable (not merely "when the local option is unset"), while PunchHole/FetchLocalAddr are steerable specifically when the local option is unset (the default). All three then reach the same unvalidated connect_tcp() sink in server.rs create_relay_connection_.
verdict.live_test: Not needed — fully confirmed statically. Optional confirmation: run the RustDesk client against a test rendezvous server that answers a legitimate hole-punch/FetchLocalAddr request with relay_server="127.0.0.1:9999" (attacker-controlled local listener), or spoof a UDP PunchHole/RequestRelay datagram at the client's rendezvous UDP port from an arbitrary source IP with relay_server pointed at an internal test IP:port. Expected vulnerable result: client opens a TCP connection to that address and writes a RequestRelay protobuf preamble (observable via a netcat listener or pcap). Expected safe result (if patched): a validation/allow-list rejection before any connect() is attempted.
verdict.observed_mitigation: none found in the traced files

candidate.title: Unauthenticated UUID_MISMATCH response lets the rendezvous server force perpetual device-ID churn
candidate.root_cause: handle_resp's RegisterPkResponse arm treats register_pk_response::Result::UUID_MISMATCH from the server as authoritative with no corroborating proof (e.g. no signature over the claim), calling handle_uuid_mismatch -> Config::update_id(), which regenerates and persists a brand-new random device ID purely on the server's say-so.
candidate.entry_point: RegisterPkResponse.result == UUID_MISMATCH from the rendezvous server.
candidate.sink: libs/hbb_common/src/config.rs Config::update_id()/Config::set_id() (~line 1279) persists a new random device ID to disk.
candidate.trace: rendezvous_mediator.rs:350-363 handle_resp matches RegisterPkResponse -> UUID_MISMATCH -> handle_uuid_mismatch (rendezvous_mediator.rs:780-793) -> config.rs:1279-1286 update_id() generates and persists a new ID.
candidate.attack: Malicious/MITM rendezvous server replies UUID_MISMATCH to every RegisterPkResponse; observed result is the client repeatedly regenerating and persisting a new numeric device ID, so its previously-shared ID becomes permanently stale/unreachable to legitimate contacts — a persistent identity-availability disruption driven purely by an unauthenticated server response.
candidate.preconditions: default config: yes.
candidate.confidence_reason: Code path is directly readable and unconditional; impact is limited to availability/identity churn rather than confidentiality or integrity of a session, and only the DoS-relevant lens explicitly requested this class of finding.

verdict.reason: Re-read rendezvous_mediator.rs in full plus the referenced config.rs and udp.rs. The claim's mechanics are accurate and directly confirmed from artifacts: handle_resp (line 361) routes register_pk_response::Result::UUID_MISMATCH straight into handle_uuid_mismatch (lines 780-793) with zero cryptographic corroboration of the server's claim, which calls Config::update_id() (config.rs:1279-1286) — this unconditionally generates a fresh random 10-digit ID via rand::thread_rng() and persists it via Config::set_id()->store() (config.rs:988-995, 718+), no throttle, no confirmation step. The SOLVING_PK_MISMATCH mutex (rendezvous_mediator.rs:782-791) is NOT a rate limiter against a single malicious host: it dedups across *different* self.host values only; once solving==self.host it stays true, so every subsequent UUID_MISMATCH from the same configured host is processed and re-churns the ID again. Default transport is UDP (Self::start, line 481-493, picks start_udp unless proxy/ws/tcp-forced), and on that path the RegisterPkResponse arrives over a plain FramedSocket with NO NaCl/secure_tcp wrapping at all (secure_tcp is only invoked in start_tcp, line 428) — so the message is both unauthenticated in content (no signature/nonce tying the response to the outstanding request) and, checking udp.rs:132-147 + rendezvous_mediator.rs:269, the sender's UDP source address returned by socket.next() is discarded at the call site (`Some(Ok((bytes, _)))`), meaning the client does not even verify the datagram came from the configured rendezvous host's address. Worse than the claim states: handle_uuid_mismatch immediately re-sends register_pk (line 792) after processing, so a malicious/on-path server can drive a self-paced, unthrottled ID-regeneration+disk-write loop bounded only by its own reply rate, not by REG_INTERVAL (15s) — REG_INTERVAL only gates the *periodic* timer-driven register_pk, not this response-triggered chain. Given the task's own stated trust model explicitly includes "rendezvous server -> client (client trusts server messages)" and "any internet host -> hbbs (pre-auth)" as in-scope attacker positions, and the mitigating checks I can point to (SOLVING_PK_MISMATCH, REG_INTERVAL backoff) do not actually bound repeated same-host abuse, this is not a "potential" issue gated behind an unobservable layer — it is directly reachable and provable from the artifacts under the stated model. That pushes it from Low/potential-Medium to a confirmed Medium: persistent identity-availability DoS (previously-shared ID goes permanently stale) plus an unthrottled disk-write amplification loop, requiring only that the client be pointed at (or MITM'd to) a malicious rendezvous host — no additional non-default precondition needed.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: handle_resp's RegisterPkResponse arm (rendezvous_mediator.rs:361) treats an unauthenticated, unsigned UUID_MISMATCH result as authoritative and calls handle_uuid_mismatch -> Config::update_id() (config.rs:1279) with no per-request nonce/signature check and no effective repeat-throttle: SOLVING_PK_MISMATCH only dedups across distinct hosts, not repeated triggers from the same host, and handle_uuid_mismatch itself immediately re-issues register_pk (line 792), creating a self-perpetuating request/response loop paced entirely by the attacker. On the default UDP transport (start_udp) this response additionally arrives with no secure_tcp/NaCl wrapping and the receive loop discards the sender's UDP source address (rendezvous_mediator.rs:269, udp.rs:132-147), so nothing ties the RegisterPkResponse to the legitimate configured server beyond destination-port delivery.
verdict.observed_mitigation: None found that actually bounds the attack: SOLVING_PK_MISMATCH (rendezvous_mediator.rs:782-791) only prevents cross-host state clobbering when the mediator is racing multiple configured rendezvous hosts simultaneously — it does not limit how many times the SAME host can trigger update_id(). REG_INTERVAL (15s, config.rs:51) only throttles the independent timer-driven register_pk retry path, not the response-triggered register_pk call inside handle_uuid_mismatch itself (line 792), which fires immediately after each processed UUID_MISMATCH.
verdict.live_test: Stand up a minimal rendezvous-protocol UDP responder that, for every incoming RegisterPk protobuf message on port 21116, immediately replies with a RendezvousMessage{RegisterPkResponse{result: UUID_MISMATCH}}. Point a RustDesk client's custom-rendezvous-server option at this responder's IP and start the client. Vulnerable result: client log shows repeated "UUID_MISMATCH received from ..." / "id updated from X to Y" lines in rapid succession (faster than the 15s REG_INTERVAL, driven purely by responder reply latency), and Config::get_id() (or the on-disk config file's `id` field) changes value repeatedly while the responder keeps replying, never converging to a stable ID. Safe/expected result on an unmodified honest server: RegisterPkResponse::OK is returned after (at most) one legitimate UUID_MISMATCH/re-register cycle, key_confirmed becomes true, and the ID stops changing.

candidate.title: Minimal-length garbage datagram spins up a full KcpEndpoint + I/O task that is held open for the full connect timeout
candidate.root_cause: KcpStream::accept in kcp_stream.rs creates and starts a full KcpEndpoint (endpoint.run().await, line 38) and spawns the kcp_io I/O task (line 52) before validating that init_packet is a legitimate KCP handshake segment -- the only check is a trivial minimum length (packet.len() >= size_of::<KcpPacketHeader>(), line 48) -- so any datagram meeting that floor consumes a full endpoint + task for up to `timeout` (CONNECT_TIMEOUT, line 54) even when the handshake can never complete.
candidate.entry_point: The first UDP datagram received by the caller (udp_nat_listen in rendezvous_mediator.rs) from the NAT-punched peer_addr, passed in as init_packet.
candidate.sink: endpoint.run().await (kcp_stream.rs:38) plus the Self::kcp_io spawn (line 52) and tokio::time::timeout(timeout, endpoint.accept()) (line 54) -- resources are held for the full timeout window per bogus datagram.
candidate.trace: attacker garbage UDP datagram (>= header size) -> udp_nat_listen (caller, after successful NAT punch) -> KcpStream::accept:37-38 (new KcpEndpoint + run) -> line 48 trivial length check passes -> line 52 kcp_io spawned -> line 54 blocks up to CONNECT_TIMEOUT waiting on endpoint.accept()
candidate.attack: A peer at the already-punched 4-tuple (or an attacker able to spoof it) repeatedly sends minimal garbage datagrams (a few bytes above header size, no valid KCP semantics) to the connected socket; each one triggers a new KcpEndpoint plus spawned I/O task that lives for the full CONNECT_TIMEOUT before failing, tying up per-connection resources on the caller for that duration for negligible attacker cost.
candidate.preconditions: Requires having reached the post-NAT-punch stage (peer_addr already resolved via rendezvous exchange); default config: yes, no additional validation exists before endpoint/task creation in any build.
candidate.potential_severity: Low-Medium -- bounded per attempt by CONNECT_TIMEOUT, but cheap and repeatable for an attacker who controls or spoofs the punched peer address, degrading legitimate connection setup latency/resources.
candidate.confidence_reason: Order of operations (endpoint creation before packet legitimacy is confirmed) is directly visible in kcp_stream.rs; real-world impact depends on how expensive KcpEndpoint::new()/run() actually is (kcp_sys internals not read).

verdict.reason: The cited code matches exactly: KcpEndpoint::new()+run() at lines 37-38 execute unconditionally, BEFORE the trivial length-only check at line 48 gates whether init_packet's bytes get forwarded, kcp_io spawns at line 52, and endpoint.accept() is bounded by tokio::time::timeout(timeout, ...) at line 54 with timeout=CONNECT_TIMEOUT=18s (confirmed in libs/hbb_common/src/config.rs:45). Reachability is real: rendezvous_mediator.rs line 386-391 spawns handle_punch_hole unconditionally for every inbound PunchHole rendezvous message with no visible client-side rate limit; handle_punch_hole -> punch_udp_hole (line 724) -> udp_nat_listen (line 948) -> socket.connect(peer_addr) -> punch_udp() (common.rs:2502, MAX_TIME=20s, returns as soon as ANY non-empty packet arrives from peer_addr) -> KcpStream::accept(..., res). So an attacker who can get the rendezvous server to relay a PunchHole naming itself, then send one garbage UDP packet to the freshly-punched socket, does reach the vulnerable accept() path pre-auth. HOWEVER the claim's attack mechanism is wrong: KcpStream::accept (and therefore KcpEndpoint::new()/run()) is called exactly ONCE per udp_nat_listen invocation (i.e. once per completed punch-hole session), not once per garbage datagram. Datagrams received after the first one, within the same session, flow into the already-spawned kcp_io task's recv_from loop (line 119-133), which applies the SAME trivial header-length floor inline (line 122) and forwards into the existing endpoint's input channel -- it does not create a new KcpEndpoint or spawn a new task. So 'repeatedly sends minimal garbage datagrams... each one triggers a new KcpEndpoint plus spawned I/O task' (claim's attack section) misdescribes the mechanism: the cost is one endpoint+task per attacker-initiated punch-hole session (which itself requires a rendezvous round trip plus a genuine UDP packet from the claimed peer address, not free/negligible repeat spam to an already-open channel), not per raw datagram.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: KcpStream::accept (kcp_stream.rs:37-38) unconditionally allocates and starts a full KcpEndpoint plus a spawned kcp_io task (line 52) before any content validation of init_packet beyond a trivial minimum-length check (line 48), then blocks up to CONNECT_TIMEOUT (18s, line 54) waiting for a real KCP handshake. This executes once per completed punch-hole session (udp_nat_listen, rendezvous_mediator.rs:948, called from handle_punch_hole with no visible client-side throttling on inbound PunchHole rendezvous messages, rendezvous_mediator.rs:386-391), reached only after punch_udp() (common.rs:2502) has already received at least one non-empty UDP packet from the claimed peer address. So the resource cost is one KcpEndpoint+task per attacker-initiated rendezvous-mediated connection attempt (bounded by how many such attempts an attacker can trigger, each needing an actual UDP round trip with the victim), not amplified per garbage datagram sent within an already-established session as the claim's 'repeatedly sends minimal garbage datagrams... each one triggers a new KcpEndpoint' framing states.
verdict.live_test: On the lab host, drive N concurrent handle_punch_hole-triggering connection attempts against a running rustdesk client instance bound to a known ID (e.g. script N separate 'connect to ID' attempts from N source ports, each following through the real rendezvous protocol so punch_udp() gets one non-empty garbage UDP datagram back), then sample the client process's thread/task count and RSS before vs during the ~18s CONNECT_TIMEOUT window. Vulnerable-result: task/thread count and memory scale roughly linearly with N concurrent sessions with no client-side cap observed; safe/mitigated-result: a cap or per-source throttle limits concurrent KcpEndpoint allocations regardless of N.
verdict.observed_mitigation: None found for the order-of-operations issue itself (endpoint creation genuinely precedes packet validation, confirmed by reading kcp_stream.rs in full). The claim's specific per-datagram amplification narrative is refuted by the code: kcp_io's own inline loop (kcp_stream.rs:119-134) handles all datagrams after the first one within a session using the existing endpoint, applying the same length floor without re-invoking KcpStream::accept or creating a new KcpEndpoint.

candidate.sink: config::LanPeers::store(&peers) in handle_received_peers (persists attacker-chosen fields to disk) and crate::flutter_ffi::main_load_lan_peers() (renders them in the LAN-peers UI); the persisted `id` is later used by send_wol()/connect flows.
candidate.trace: src/lan.rs:238 socket.recv_from() (any LAN source) -> src/lan.rs:239-243 Message::parse_from_bytes + match cmd=="pong" (no source auth) -> src/lan.rs:266-276 tx.send(DiscoveryPeer{id:p.id, hostname:p.hostname, username:p.username, platform:p.platform, ip_mac:{addr.ip():p.mac}, online:true}) forwards raw attacker fields -> src/lan.rs:316-331 handle_received_peers prepends into `peers` and calls config::LanPeers::store(&peers) + crate::flutter_ffi::main_load_lan_peers()

verdict.reason:
Read the full file (targets/rustdesk/src/lan.rs) plus the call chain into it and out of it. The claim holds up exactly as stated:

1. `wait_response` (lines 221-288) runs on the ephemeral, `SO_BROADCAST`-enabled sockets created by `send_query()`/`create_broadcast_sockets()` when the local client itself initiates a LAN scan — a *separate* code path from `start_listening()` (the `enable-lan-discovery`-gated server side in `rendezvous_mediator.rs:143`). There is no `enable-lan-discovery` gate, no source-IP/MAC allowlist, and no cryptographic check anywhere in `wait_response` before a `pong` is accepted (lines 241-277).

2. The only comparison present (`local_mac.is_empty() && p.mac.is_empty() || local_mac != p.mac`, line 265) is a self-echo filter (skip a pong whose MAC equals the host's own interface MAC), not a sender-authentication control — trivially bypassed by sending any MAC that isn't the victim's own.

3. All attacker-supplied fields (`p.id`, `p.hostname`, `p.username`, `p.platform`, `p.mac`) are forwarded verbatim into `config::DiscoveryPeer` and sent over the channel (lines 266-276) — verified against `DiscoveryPeer`'s definition in `libs/hbb_common/src/config.rs:2280-2298`, which has zero validation (`is_same_peer` only compares `id`+`username`, itself attacker-controlled).

4. `handle_received_peers` (lines 305-344) inserts the unauthenticated peer at position 0 and calls `config::LanPeers::store(&peers)` (persists to disk) and `crate::flutter_ffi::main_load_lan_peers()` (refreshes UI) exactly as claimed.

5. Reachability/default-config confirmed via the Flutter/Dart side: `DiscoveredPeersView.build()` in `flutter/lib/common/widgets/peers_view.dart:505-510` calls `bind.mainDiscover()` (→ `crate::lan::discover()` → `wait_response`) on every rebuild of the "Discovered" tab — no explicit button click required, just having that tab visible. That tab is enabled by default (`flutter/lib/models/peer_tab_model.dart:43`: `!isWeb && ... != "Y"`), i.e. it ships on by default on desktop and is only off if an operator explicitly sets `disable-discovery-panel=Y`. This confirms the claim's precondition and "default config: yes" assertion, and actually shows the exposure window recurs on every tab rebuild rather than being a single momentary click.

No mitigating control exists in the read code — the root cause, entry point, trace, and sink are all accurately described and directly observable in the artifacts. This is genuinely unauthenticated UDP peer-discovery spoofing that reaches persisted config + UI by default. Severity: agree with the original Medium rating (confirmed real, provable, exploitable spoofing primitive) with "potential High" appropriately hedged, since realizing meaningful impact (session hijack/phishing-to-connect) still requires a subsequent victim click plus normal RustDesk connection/auth flow to the attacker's real ID — this bug delivers identity-spoofing/list-poisoning, not a direct auth bypass or RCE by itself.
verdict.observed_mitigation: None found in the read code beyond a self-echo MAC filter (line 265) which is not a sender-authentication control and is trivially bypassed.
verdict.live_test: Not required for confirmation — fully provable from static artifacts (Rust source path + Dart binding call site + default tab-enablement flag). Optional live confirmation for extra assurance: on a LAN, run the RustDesk desktop client, open the 'Discovered' peer tab (triggers bind.mainDiscover()); from a second LAN host, craft and unicast a RendezvousMessage{PeerDiscovery{cmd:'pong', id:'999999999', hostname:'IT-Support', username:'Administrator', platform:'Windows 11 Pro', mac:'AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF'}} (protobuf-serialized per libs/hbb_common/protos/rendezvous.proto) directly to the source UDP port seen in the client's broadcast 'ping' packet (captured via tcpdump on the broadcast port RENDEZVOUS_PORT+3). Vulnerable result: entry 'IT-Support / Administrator' with id 999999999 appears in the client's Discovered list and persists in the _lan_peers config file after the scan window closes. Safe/patched result: unsolicited/unverified pong from a non-matching sender is rejected and never appears in the list.

candidate.entry_point: Flood of RendezvousMessage::PeerDiscovery{cmd:'pong', id:<unique per packet>, ...} datagrams from an attacker-controlled LAN host, forwarded through the unbounded mpsc channel from wait_response.

verdict.reason:
Read the full file. The claim's mechanism is exactly as described and provable purely from the static code with no unobserved-layer assumptions:

- `wait_response` (lines 236-286) is fed by per-broadcast-socket threads spawned from `spawn_wait_responses` (lines 290-303), each running until 3s of silence — but `last_recv_time` resets on every received packet (line 242), so a continuously-flooding attacker can keep the thread alive indefinitely.
- The forward-to-channel gate at lines 265-276 (`local_mac.is_empty() && p.mac.is_empty() || local_mac != p.mac`) only filters out an exact-mac-match reflection of the victim's own probe; an attacker on the LAN trivially satisfies `local_mac != p.mac` by sending any mac (or empty mac when victim's local mac happens non-empty), so arbitrary spoofed `PeerDiscovery{cmd:"pong", id:<attacker-chosen>, ...}` packets reach the unbounded `mpsc` channel.
- In `handle_received_peers` (lines 305-344): `response_set.insert(peer.id.clone())` (311/317) is only used to decide whether to *merge* `ip_mac`/set `online=true` on a re-seen id — it does not gate insertion. `DiscoveryPeer::is_same_peer` (config.rs:1737-1739) matches on `id == id && username == username`, so any attacker-chosen distinct `id` (or same id with a different `username`) fails the `position()` lookup at line 318, and execution falls straight through to the unconditional `peers.insert(0, peer)` at line 325 — confirmed exact line match. There is no cap, no LRU eviction, no per-source rate limit anywhere in this function or in `config::LanPeers` (config.rs:1742-1767): `LanPeers::store()` just serializes whatever `Vec<DiscoveryPeer>` it's given, no size check.
- The growing vec is persisted to disk every ~300ms while flooding continues (line 326-327/`config::LanPeers::store(&peers)`) and again unconditionally when the loop exits (line 340) — so bloat outlives the session, confirming the claim's "bloats persisted state" language, not just transient memory growth.
- Reachability is real and slightly broader than the claim states: `discover()`/`handle_received_peers` is invoked from `DiscoveredPeersView.build()` in flutter/lib/common/widgets/peers_view.dart:505-511 (`bind.mainDiscover()`), which fires on ordinary widget rebuild of the "Discovered" peers tab (a default UI tab, gated only by the client-side `disable-discovery-panel` option, not `enable-lan-discovery`). The `enable-lan-discovery` check in lan.rs only gates the *responder* path (`start_listening`, line 38-43) that answers other hosts' pings — it does not gate the vulnerable requester/aggregation path at all, so this is reachable by default whenever a user views the Discovered/LAN tab, no special config required.

No mitigating check, cap, or rate limiter exists anywhere in the cited code path or in the `LanPeers` config type. This is a genuine, statically-provable DoS via unbounded attacker-controlled Vec growth + disk persistence, matching the claim's root cause, trace, and sink almost exactly. Severity as scoped (Low actual / Medium potential, given the LAN-adjacency and UI-open precondition, non-memory-corruption DoS impact) is reasonable and not being corrected.

candidate.entry_point: Attacker-controlled `RegisterPk{id, uuid, pk}` protobuf field values delivered over the plaintext, unauthenticated UDP rendezvous socket (trust boundary: any internet host -> hbbs, pre-auth).
candidate.sink: self.pm.update_pk(id, peer, addr, rk.uuid, rk.pk, ip) at rendezvous_server.rs:418, which overwrites the peer's stored public key that is later signed and handed out by get_pk() (used to vouch for the peer's identity during PunchHole/RelayResponse key exchange).
candidate.trace: UDP datagram -> RendezvousServer::handle_udp (rendezvous_server.rs ~324) -> RegisterPk match arm (~342) -> uuid==rk.uuid but only-pk-differs branch skips the UUID_MISMATCH early-return (~359-371) -> changed=true (~383-386) -> self.pm.update_pk(...) (~418) -> subsequent self.get_pk() (~1195-1218) signs and serves the attacker's pk as authoritative for that id.
candidate.attack: The uuid field is sent in cleartext over unauthenticated UDP (no NaCl channel on this path), so any on-path attacker (rogue Wi-Fi/gateway/ISP MITM sitting between a legitimate client and hbbs — squarely within the stated trust boundary 'any internet host -> hbbs/hbbr (pre-auth)') can passively capture a legitimate RegisterPk packet to learn {id, uuid}. The attacker then sends its own RegisterPk{id, uuid: <captured>, pk: <attacker pk>} to hbbs, sourced (naturally, since it is on-path) from the same IP hbbs already associates with that peer. Because the ip-unchanged branch of the guard never checks pk equality on its own, the server accepts the new pk and calls update_pk, permanently replacing the legitimate device's server-attested public key with the attacker's. Requires attacker to be on-path between a legitimate client and hbbs (or otherwise able to source-match the peer's last-registered IP) and to have observed one legitimate RegisterPk packet for the target id.
candidate.confidence_reason: The flawed `&&` guard and the plaintext/unauthenticated nature of the UDP RegisterPk path are both directly visible and unambiguous in the read source; residual uncertainty is only about how easy it is in practice for a given attacker to become on-path or IP-match, which is an external/network precondition, not a code question.

verdict.reason:
Re-read rendezvous_server.rs in full and the peer.rs / .proto companions. The claim's central assertion is verified byte-for-byte against the source:

1. Guard logic (rendezvous_server.rs:359-371, inside `handle_udp`'s `RegisterPk` arm): when `peer.uuid == rk.uuid`, the ONLY rejection path is `if peer.info.ip != ip && peer.pk != rk.pk { ... return UUID_MISMATCH }`. This is a strict AND — if the source IP matches the peer's last-stored `peer.info.ip` but `rk.pk` differs from `peer.pk`, the `if` body is skipped and execution falls through with no rejection. There is no other check anywhere in this arm (lines 342-426) that independently validates the new pk against the old one.

2. Fallthrough consequence (lines 382-387): `let ip_changed = peer.info.ip != ip;` then `changed = peer.pk != rk.pk || ip_changed` (the `peer.uuid != rk.uuid` disjunct is always false inside this branch since we're already inside `if peer.uuid == rk.uuid`). So a same-IP, different-pk registration sets `changed = true`.

3. Sink (line 418): `if changed { self.pm.update_pk(id, peer, addr, rk.uuid, rk.pk, ip).await; }`. Traced into peer.rs:93-133 `PeerMap::update_pk` — it unconditionally does `w.pk = pk.clone()` and persists via `db.update_pk`/`db.insert_peer`, no proof-of-possession of the old private key is required (RegisterPk carries no signature — confirmed in libs/hbb_common/protos/rendezvous.proto:58-63, just `id`, `uuid` (bytes), `pk` (bytes), `old_id`, all plaintext protobuf over unauthenticated UDP).

4. Downstream trust: `get_pk` (rendezvous_server.rs:1196-1218) reads `peer.pk` straight from the map and server-signs `{id, pk}` with the server's sign key; this signed blob is handed out via PunchHoleResponse/RelayResponse (call sites at lines 512, 625, 659). So the substituted pk becomes the server-attested identity key for that ID going forward — exactly as the claim states.

5. Checked for a mitigating layer: `check_ip_blocker` (lines 883-911) is a pure rate-limiter (counts registrations per IP/day), not a cryptographic or identity check — it does not close this gap. No other guard exists in the file for this arm.

6. Confirmed this is genuine, unmodified upstream code: `git log` in targets/rustdesk-server shows origin github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk-server, HEAD 91fb928 (2026-07-07), not a synthetic/injected-bug fixture.

The entry point is directly attacker-reachable: `handle_udp` parses `RendezvousMessage` straight off the raw UDP socket with no prior authentication (confirmed at lines 317-345), consistent with the stated trust boundary "any internet host -> hbbs (pre-auth)".

The claim's stated preconditions (attacker must know the target's uuid — learnable by passively observing one cleartext RegisterPk packet — and must present a source IP matching the peer's last-registered IP, via on-path position, shared-NAT co-location, or off-path UDP source spoofing since no response is needed to complete the state change) are accurate, not overclaimed, and are honestly reflected in the claim's own preconditions/confidence (0.8) rather than hand-waved as default/trivial. This is provable entirely from the artifacts in front of me with no reliance on an unobserved runtime layer, so this does not require needs-live-validation — it is confirmed. Severity Critical is defensible: successful exploitation lets the attacker become the server-attested holder of a live RustDesk ID, enabling MITM/hijack of that ID's future PunchHole/Relay key exchanges — a break of the core identity-pinning guarantee the rendezvous service exists to provide, with a scope change into the downstream peer-to-peer session security.
verdict.observed_mitigation: check_ip_blocker (rendezvous_server.rs:883-911) provides only per-IP/per-day registration-count rate limiting; it is not a cryptographic or identity check and does not prevent the same-IP pk-substitution path. No other mitigating check exists in the RegisterPk arm.
verdict.live_test: Not required for the verdict (mechanism is fully provable from source), but a safe confirmatory test: stand up hbbs in the lab; from host A send RegisterPk{id="X", uuid=U, pk=PK1} (establishes peer X with uuid U, pk PK1, ip=A); then from a second source that the server observes as the same IP A (e.g. same container/NAT, or loopback-adjacent test harness spoofing source to A) send RegisterPk{id="X", uuid=U, pk=PK2}. Vulnerable: server responds OK (register_pk_response::Result::OK) and a subsequent GetPk-triggering flow (e.g. RequestRelay or PunchHoleSent for id X) returns a signature over PK2, not PK1. Safe/patched: server would return UUID_MISMATCH on the second RegisterPk despite the IP match.

candidate.entry_point: Arbitrary UDP datagram delivered to the client's rendezvous UDP socket, parsed as a `RendezvousMessage`; specifically the `ConfigureUpdate{serial, rendezvous_servers}` variant.
candidate.sink: Config::set_option("rendezvous-servers", cu.rendezvous_servers.join(",")) in rendezvous_mediator.rs:409-412, which persists via config.rs Config::set_option (~1259-1277) -> config.store() to disk, followed by Self::restart() when the value changed.
candidate.trace: spoofed/MITM UDP packet -> socket.next() (rendezvous_mediator.rs:267-269, source addr discarded) -> Message::parse_from_bytes -> RendezvousMediator::handle_resp (~271) -> ConfigureUpdate arm (~407-417) -> Config::set_option (config.rs ~1259) -> config.store() persists to disk -> Self::restart() reconnects using the attacker-supplied server list.

candidate.confidence_reason: The missing sender-address check and the persisted, unauthenticated ConfigureUpdate sink are both directly visible in the read files; the only unverified detail (outside these 4 files) is whether the underlying UDP socket is connect()-ed, which would narrow this from blind-off-path spoofing to on-path-only MITM, but does not change that no application-layer check exists.

(1) rendezvous_mediator.rs:267-269 confirms the source-address tuple element is discarded (`Some(Ok((bytes, _)))`) before `Message::parse_from_bytes` -> `handle_resp`. (2) rendezvous_mediator.rs:407-417 confirms ConfigureUpdate unconditionally calls `Config::set_option(\"rendezvous-servers\", ...)` and `Config::set_serial(cu.serial)` with no origin/signature check, then `Self::restart()` if the resolved list changed. verdict.live_test: Lab setup (safe, local-only): run a rustdesk client built from this tree with `custom-rendezvous-server` unset (default), pointed via `/etc/hosts` or `--server` at a rendezvous host you control, on an isolated network namespace/VM so no real traffic leaves the lab. verdict.observed_mitigation: None for the default configuration/transport. Two mitigations exist but do not apply by default: (1) the TCP rendezvous transport (`is_proxy()`/`use_ws()`/`is_udp_disabled()` = true) runs `secure_tcp`, which cryptographically authenticates the server via NaCl signature verification against a pinned key before any ConfigureUpdate is trusted — but UDP is the default transport and skips this entirely. (2) an enterprise/managed deployment that has pre-populated `OVERWRITE_SETTINGS` for the `rendezvous-servers` key (via `is_option_can_save`, config.rs:2760-2772) would have the malicious write silently dropped — but this is an opt-in admin-pushed policy, not present in an unmanaged/default install.

verdict.reason:
The core data-flow claim is verified: connection_meta() in rendezvous_mediator.rs (lines 36-44, called at 503-506/582-585/661-664) builds ConnectionMeta straight from PunchHole/RequestRelay/FetchLocalAddr.control_permissions and .controlled_context — untrusted fields the reference rendezvous_server.rs (targets/rustdesk-server/src/rendezvous_server.rs) never populates (grep confirms zero references to these fields there, so any non-default value is server-forged). This ConnectionMeta is threaded into crate::accept_connection / create_relay_connection / create_tcp_connection, which land in server/connection.rs::Connection::start (line 452), confirming the claim's cited sinks are real and the trace is accurate.

However, tracing further into server/connection.rs (outside the 4 originally-cited files, which the claim itself flagged as unverified) shows the actual authorization semantics are narrower than 'auth-bypass'/'maximal full-control access':
1. self.authorized only ever becomes true via send_logon_response_and_keep_alive() (line 1657), reached only after real password validation (validate_password(), line 2727) or an existing recent-session token — control_permissions never sets self.authorized directly. So the rendezvous server CANNOT grant a session without a valid password or local user click-approval; core authentication is intact.
2. What control_permissions actually does: Self::permission() (connection.rs:2388-2418) lets any explicitly-set bit (enable OR disable) completely override Self::is_permission_enabled_locally() — i.e. the LOCAL device owner's configured policy — for 8 granular session capabilities (keyboard, clipboard, audio, file, restart, recording, block_input, privacy_mode), computed once at Connection::start (lines 520-528) directly from the untrusted meta, with no tie back to the device's own config. This is a real, confirmable bug: a rogue/MITM rendezvous server can silently force-enable block_input, privacy_mode, restart, recording, clipboard, file-transfer, audio, or keyboard capabilities beyond what the local admin configured, for a session that a human/credential still had to approve.
3. Additionally, for the pre-auth login-request-type gate (file-transfer/view-camera/terminal/port-forward at lines 2533-2582), a forged control_permissions bit can bypass the early 'feature disabled locally' hard-reject and let the connection proceed into the normal password-validation flow instead — but the attacker still must supply/guess the correct password or get local click-approval afterward, so this alone grants no access.

Net: the claim's mechanism (untrusted rendezvous fields flowing unchecked into local session policy) is real and reproducible from artifacts, but the bug_class/root_cause/severity are overstated — it is a local-security-policy-override for capability toggles on an already-authenticated/approved session (and a minor pre-auth type-gate bypass that still requires valid credentials), not an authentication bypass granting 'maximal/full-control access'.

verdict.reason:
Re-derived from source and the claim's core mechanics hold, but it under-states severity and slightly mis-frames the "reflection" angle as secondary when it is actually the most solid, fully-provable-from-artifacts part of the bug.

Verified facts (all from artifacts I read, not assumed):
1. handle_hole_sent (rendezvous_server.rs:608-639) and handle_local_addr (:642-671), reached unauthenticated from raw UDP via handle_udp's PunchHoleSent/LocalAddr arms (:431-436), compute the send destination as `addr_a = AddrMangle::decode(&phs.socket_addr)` / `&la.socket_addr` — a field taken verbatim from the incoming datagram — and send with `socket.send(&msg_out, addr_a)` (line 634 for hole_sent, matches claim exactly; ~666 for local_addr). No lookup against any prior PunchHole/FetchLocalAddr session, no correlation to the actual UDP source `addr`, no PUNCH_REQS check (that table is written only by the TCP-only handle_punch_hole_request path and is never read by these two handlers).
2. AddrMangle (libs/hbb_common/src/lib.rs:127-185) is NOT a keyed/authenticated token — encode()/decode() is a public, deterministic, secret-free arithmetic transform (attacker picks their own `tm`, e.g. 0, and can forge a valid encoding for ANY target IPv4/IPv6+port from scratch, offline, using only the public formula). So `addr_a` is fully attacker-chosen with certainty, not merely "probably."
3. get_pk (rendezvous_server.rs:1196-1218) signs an IdPk{id, pk} with the server's real ed25519 secret key for whatever `id` the attacker supplies, provided `version` is non-empty (trivial) and `self.inner.sk` is Some. Default config (`get_arg_or("key","-".to_owned())` in main.rs:35 → get_server_sk() with key=="-") auto-generates/loads a real signing key, so sk is Some by default — this precondition is NOT a non-default requirement, contrary to what a lazy reader might assume.
4. PeerMap::get (peer.rs:139-150) checks the in-memory map AND falls back to the persistent DB, so `id` need not be a currently-online peer — any peer that ever registered qualifies, widening the oracle beyond "current sessions."
5. Crucially, this UDP path requires NO IP-spoofing capability by the attacker: the destination is a message-body field, not derived from the packet's source IP, so it works even on networks with BCP38 egress filtering — a stronger/easier primitive than classic UDP reflection DDoS. There is also no rate limiting on this path (unlike RegisterPk's check_ip_blocker).
6. Corroborating evidence the developers of this codebase already recognize this bug class: the sibling UDP PunchHoleRequest handler was explicitly disabled with the comment "UDP PunchHoleRequest is intentionally unsupported. The supported client path sends PunchHoleRequest over TCP/WS." (rendezvous_server.rs:427-430) — a hardening step for exactly this shape of issue — yet PunchHoleSent/LocalAddr, which have the identical "attacker-named arbitrary destination, unconditional send" shape, were left wired on UDP. This is strong circumstantial confirmation of an oversight rather than a hypothetical.

What remains genuinely unverifiable from these 4 files (server-side only): whether a real RustDesk client, upon receiving an unsolicited PunchHoleResponse it never requested, would act on the embedded signed pk/relay_server/nat_type in a way that enables session confusion/MITM. That client-trust question is outside rendezvous_server.rs and stays a "needs-live-validation" sub-claim, exactly as the original author flagged. But the reflection/redirection primitive itself — an unauthenticated party using hbbs as a stateless UDP traffic generator that will emit a real, server-signed packet at any chosen internet address with no spoofing required and no rate limit — is fully confirmed by static reading alone and does not depend on that unseen layer.

Net: claim's root cause and trace are accurate and precisely cited (line 608/634 match source exactly). It should be corrected upward from Medium to High given (a) no spoofing needed, (b) no rate limiting on this path, (c) default-config sk presence, (d) DB-wide id scope, and (e) the sibling-handler hardening comment showing this exact bug class was already on the developers' radar but not fully remediated. The "session hijack/impersonation" sub-claim stays speculative pending live client testing.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: handle_hole_sent/handle_local_addr in rendezvous_server.rs derive the UDP send destination solely from an unauthenticated, non-cryptographic, attacker-forgeable AddrMangle-encoded field inside the incoming PunchHoleSent/LocalAddr message, with zero binding to (a) the actual UDP source address of the sender, (b) any session/nonce from a prior legitimate PunchHoleRequest, or (c) PUNCH_REQS state (which these handlers never consult). Because AddrMangle::encode/decode (hbb_common/src/lib.rs) uses no secret key, any unauthenticated internet host can forge a valid encoding for an arbitrary victim IP:port entirely offline, with no source-IP spoofing required — a materially easier and less-mitigable primitive than typical UDP reflection bugs. Combined with get_pk() unconditionally signing an IdPk for any attacker-supplied id found in-memory OR in the persistent peer DB (peer.rs PeerMap::get), using a real ed25519 key that is present by default (main.rs default key="-" auto-generates sk), this lets any unauthenticated UDP sender make hbbs emit a genuine, server-signed, unsolicited packet at any chosen third-party address, unrate-limited. verdict.reason:
Re-read the full file (rendezvous_server.rs, lines 1-1364) plus AddrMangle (libs/hbb_common/src/lib.rs:111-185) and the RelayResponse/RequestRelay/PunchHoleRequest proto definitions. The claim holds up exactly as stated, with no mitigating check anywhere:

1. The RelayResponse arm (line 507-526) decodes `addr_b = AddrMangle::decode(&rr.socket_addr)` purely from client-supplied bytes and immediately calls `self.send_to_tcp_sync(msg_out, addr_b)` (line 525) → `self.tcp_punch.lock().await.remove(&try_into_v4(addr))` (line 843) → whatever Sink is stored there gets the message. There is zero comparison between the sending connection's own `addr` and `addr_b`, zero session/nonce token, and zero check that this TCP connection was ever the legitimate recipient of the RequestRelay/PunchHoleRequest that populated that `tcp_punch` entry.
2. `rr.id` (line 510-514, a `oneof` field per rendezvous.proto:114-125) and `rr.relay_server` (line 516-523) are both taken from the attacker's own message and used to build the message forwarded to whoever sits at `addr_b` — `get_pk` signs whatever `id` string is supplied against the peer map, and the `relay_server` override only fires for the LAN case or when it equals `self.inner.local_ip`; any other attacker-chosen relay_server string passes through unchanged (line 520-523), confirming the claim's "attacker-influenced id/relay_server" detail.
3. Unlike PunchHoleRequest (line 682, `ph.licence_key != key` gate), the RelayResponse arm has **no license-key check at all** — RelayResponse doesn't even have a `licence_key` field in the proto (rendezvous.proto:114-125) — so this path is reachable by any TCP-connected client in default config, confirming the claim's precondition statement.
4. `AddrMangle::encode/decode` (lib.rs:127-185) is a keyless, unauthenticated, purely arithmetic obfuscation (timestamp-mixed but no server secret/HMAC) that is public source shared with the client — so an attacker doesn't need to intercept any server message to construct a valid encoding for an arbitrary chosen IP:port; they only need to know that IP:port. This is a detail the claim under-leveraged (it makes the "forge socket_addr" step trivial, not merely difficult) — a correction in the claim's favor.

I found no code-level barrier that refutes the claim. The one place the claim is slightly imprecise: it characterizes the exploitability gate as "a live-race/timing precondition" — more precisely it is a *knowledge* precondition (attacker must know the victim's live server-observed IP:port, i.e., ephemeral TCP source port, while that connection's `tcp_punch` entry is still present, a window that lasts up to the 30s read-timeout in handle_listener_inner or until the entry is consumed/closed). That's a real, non-vacuous barrier for a blind attacker-vs-arbitrary-stranger scenario, but it evaporates entirely when the attacker is the legitimate target peer B chosen by victim A (B already legitimately receives A's AddrMangle-encoded address via the forwarded PunchHoleRequest/RequestRelay, so no guessing is needed at all) — in that sub-case the bug degrades to unauthenticated id/pk/relay_server injection within a session B is already part of, which is unconditionally exploitable with zero preconditions beyond being contacted once.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: Same as claimed (unauthenticated, session-token-free `tcp_punch` lookup keyed only by an attacker-decodable IP:port, with attacker-controlled id/pk/relay_server fields on the RelayResponse arm of handle_tcp), with two refinements: (a) AddrMangle is a keyless/unauthenticated public encoding, so forging `socket_addr` for a target the attacker already knows the address of is trivial, not merely "possible"; (b) the exploitation precondition is more precisely "attacker must know the victim's live server-observed ephemeral TCP source/port" rather than a generic timing race — this precondition is fully bypassed (zero cost) when the attacker is the legitimate target peer B that the victim A actually tried to connect to, since B legitimately receives A's encoded address via the normal PunchHoleRequest/RequestRelay forward and can then inject a forged id/pk/relay_server into that exchange with no guessing required.
verdict.corrected_severity: Medium (matches claim); the always-available zero-precondition sub-case (attacker as legitimate target peer B forging id/pk/relay_server back to the requester A) supports at least Medium with no live-race caveat, while the blind arbitrary-third-party redirect variant remains gated by ephemeral-port knowledge and stays in the claim's stated Medium/High(potential) band.
verdict.live_test:
Build hbbs from targets/rustdesk-server with no --key set (default, unauthenticated). Using a small harness linking hbb_common (or a Python script with protoc-compiled message_pb2/rendezvous_pb2 stubs matching libs/hbb_common/protos/*.proto), framed per bytes_codec.rs (4-byte length prefix + protobuf bytes) over TCP to 127.0.0.1:21116:
1. Conn A: connect, send RendezvousMessage{union: PunchHoleRequest{id:"nonexistent-a", version:""}}. Do NOT read a response yet — this both inserts A's sink into tcp_punch (rendezvous_server.rs:487-488) and (since 'nonexistent-a' won't resolve) leaves the connection idle with the tcp_punch entry intact. Record A's local ephemeral port via the socket's local_addr() (this is the value a real attacker would otherwise have to know/guess).
2. Conn B (separate, unrelated TCP connection, never sent any PunchHoleRequest/RequestRelay referencing A): send RendezvousMessage{union: RelayResponse{socket_addr: AddrMangle::encode(127.0.0.1:<A's port>), id:"attacker-claimed-id", relay_server:"attacker-relay.example:9999"}}.
3. On Conn A, read the next inbound frame with a 2s timeout.
Vulnerable result: Conn A receives a RelayResponse message carrying B's injected id/pk/relay_server, proving the server delivered a message from an unrelated, non-participating connection straight into A's pending slot with no binding check. Safe/patched result: Conn A gets nothing (timeout) because the server rejects RelayResponse from a connection that never legitimately received/owned that target address (e.g., via a per-transaction token echoed from the original PunchHoleRequest/RequestRelay).
verdict.observed_mitigation: None found. Read the entirety of handle_tcp (lines 475-561), send_to_tcp / send_to_tcp_sync (813-846), handle_punch_hole_request (674-782), AddrMangle::encode/decode (hbb_common/src/lib.rs:127-185), and the RelayResponse/RequestRelay/PunchHoleRequest proto message definitions — no session token, nonce, sender-address comparison, or license-key gate exists on the RelayResponse code path.
